speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege which affects the rights and privileges of every member of this House, and I raise this matter at the earliest possible moment. My question of privilege relates to a return tabled in the Commons yesterday for the Conservative member for Cumberland-Col-chester North (Mr. Coates).
The information given in the Commons return states that 11 of 13 ministers have offices in federal buildings but the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) rents an office at $7,360 a year in his Montreal Mount Royal riding, and the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier) rents an office in Montreal Maisonneuve at $1,675 a year. The President of the Privy Council (Mr. Macdonald) and the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Andras) pay their one-man staffs in their ridings, Toronto Rosedale and Port Arthur respectively, up to $10,000 annually out of the public treasury. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) is the only minister with a two-member staff in his riding, Medicine Hat. Each is paid up to $5,000 annually.
The Prime Minister's and the Secretary of State's constituency staffers each receive $7,500 annually at the maximum. Other ministers with constituency offices and the maximum publicly paid salaries for their staffers are as follows: The Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson), Kingston, $7,500; the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Greene), Niagara Falls, $7,500; the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Cote), Longueuil, $7,500; the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey), Verdun, $7,500; the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford), Vancouver Centre, $5,000; the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin), Drummondville, $5,000; the Minister of Communications (Mr. Kierans), Montreal Duvemay, $7,500; and the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. MacEachen), the only Nova Scotian, no publicly paid staff.
There is the economy drive.

Mr. Speaker, in view of the economy drive and in view of these facts as tabled in the Commons I therefore move: That the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections consider whether members of the Queen's Privy Council for Canada holding offices as Ministers of the Crown have violated the provisions of the Senate and House of Commons Act respecting the independence of Parliament by accepting allowances and profits out of public moneys to purposes not authorized by vote of this House.
Hear, hear.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I ask leave to move the adjournment of the

April 14, 1970
House under Standing Order 26 for the purpose of discussing a specific and important matter requiring urgent consideration, namely, the new situation created by the final breakdown of negotiations between the government anid the Montreal postal mail truck drivers and the announcement of the government to hire a new staff tomorrow to replace the present employees, which will bring great hardship to them and may lead to a complete disruption of mail services with its consequent serious effect on the entire population of Montreal.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE MONTREAL POSTAL DISPUTE
speechtext:
Hon. members who have heard the proposed motion will agree, I am sure, that this motion is deserving of the most serious and careful consideration. The substantive aspects of the matter which is suggested for discussion later today under Standing Order 26 cannot be overlooked and their importance cannot be minimized.
At the same time, the decision which the Chair has to make in such circumstances is essentially a procedural one, taking into account the limitations prescribed by the Standing Order.
Some weeks ago the hon. member for Peace River proposed the adjournment of the House under Standing Order 26 for the purpose of discussing the postal situation in Montreal. This motion was granted and a debate ensued. Then on April 6 the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands asked leave to move the adjournment of the House to discuss the Montreal postal situation and, to quote the hon. member, "the need for Parliament to consider alternative courses of action". This motion was denied, having regard to subsection (d) of section 16 of Standing Order 26 which reads as follows:
(d) the motion must not revive discussion on a matter which has been discussed in the same session pursuant to the provisions of this Standing Order;
Thus, the Standing Order prescribes that there can be only one emergency debate about a given situation during a session of Parliament. On this basis, the proposed motion had to be refused. The ruling of the Chair did indicate that there may be a point in the course of a developing situation where new aspects, new factors or new facts would justify a second debate in the sense that the House would then be dealing with a new situation.
The question to be resolved in this respect is: when does a continuing emergency become a new emergency so that a debate would not
Montreal Postal Dispute in effect revive discussion on a matter which has already been discussed in a previous emergency debate? The answer is not entirely clear to me in the light of the circumstances as they exist today.
Without reaching a conclusion on this aspect of Standing Order 26, I remind hon. members of the other difficulty provided by the Standing Order. The rule enjoins the Speaker to consider whether the matter can be brought before the House within a reasonable time by other means. Since it has been agreed that there will be a continuation of the budget debate tomorrow, I cannot ignore the fact that this will automatically provide an opportunity for debate within 24 hours. I do not see how the Chair can overlook this aspect of the relevant Standing Order. Therefore, taking into account mainly the fact that there is an opportunity for debate as early as tomorrow, I must conclude that the motion should not be put today. At the same time, I can assure hon. members that I will not feel so strictly bound by subsection (d) of section 16 of Standing Order 26 that an emergency debate on the situation might not be possible later.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last night I inadvertently became involved in this debate because of the lack of farmers in the House. As a result, I have had a look at this bill and I now want to say only a few things about it.
In the last few years there has been considerable agitation for changes in the handling of grain, not the least of which has been the operation LIFT program which, in effect, will take wheat out of production this year and put the land into summerfallow. This would establish in Canada the basis for an opportunity to start handling sales in a different manner. If this program is totally satisfactory then the new Canada Grain Act will have provided a new basis for the grain trade.
Presumably this is good legislation because it has a number of potentials. However, it also has some weaknesses. These weaknesses, in many cases, stem from the fact this is open ended legislation. This piece of legislation, along with other legislative measures necessary for western Canada will obviously

April 14, 1970
Canada Grain Act
change the whole structure for marketing grain. This measure will undoubtedly be considered in the light of our ability to subsidize agricultural production. As an industrial nation, we have for 20 years paid-up service to the concept of developing cheap food, but we have not supplied food at cost as have other countries. Certainly France, the United States and Great Britain have done this for years, as have other agricultural countries. They have subsidized agricultural production. We have done things a little differenily. We have not even asked the people receiving the benefits of low cost production to pay the subsidy out of the general treasury; we have asked the farmer to pay this subsidy out of his pocket. We have not done much, nor will we do much in this bill, to assist the farmer in getting a better price for his produce.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
The legislation we are now considering, and the marketing legislation which is next on the Order Paper, should be geared to the development of a new marketing structure. If these measures are successful, they should provide the producer with a better return on his production. It has been pointed out by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, and I will not quote their figures because hon. members have had an opportunity of considering their brief recently submitted to cabinet, that most farmers in Canada receive less than $2,500 annual cash income. The federation points out that less than 50 per cent of Canadian farmers receive more than $5,000 in annual cash income. The agriculture industry certainly is not in good shape and there must be some reason for this.
On a number of occasions I have had the opportunity of accompanying the agriculture committee to the offices of the Board of Grain Commissioners in Winnipeg. We have had numerous discussions and discovered the complexity of the grading system which has grown up over the years. Under this system, we find there are 400 grades of grain. Obviously, these 400 grades do not fit into either domestic or international price categories. They are grades established in respect of specific conditions. They have become so complex they are of no real value to the producer in assessing the grade he may expect, and of no value to the government in establishing a grade that is generally understood in the export market.
I remember a former Minister of Agriculture saying in this House that everyone knew Canada had the best wheat in the world and 
wheat of the highest protein content. These people have not beaten a pathway to our door to buy wheat. They have not really been convinced of the superiority of Canadian wheat. If they have been convinced, they have not been interested because the price was not right or because the commodity did not meet their needs. There is a chart on the wall of the grain commissioners offices which allows them to ascertain the exact protein content of wheat from a given area. They know the area protein content of this year's crop, and as soon as the new crop is ready for harvest they can make a decision and a projection for the following crop year.
We have been playing around with protein content and yet a decision has not been made in respect of whether we are to establish protein content as the major factor in our selling machinery or whether we are to establish another grading system. I am concerned, as I am sure many other farmers are, about what the international grading system is. For instance, what grading system is used by Australia, Russia or Great Britain; what is the relationship between protein and the type of wheat the markets of the world want; what is the ultimate protein content for wheat; what is the protein content for bread and what is the most advantageous method by which to establish a grade? As was pointed out by speakers last night, our export sales have dropped considerably from what they were three years ago. Certainly, we are down considerably both in our ability to sell and in our ability to receive a reasonable price that would equal our cost of production.
I agree with the minister that if we are unable to sell wheat at a reasonable price, then we might as well take it out of production and ask our farmers to switch to something else. But before that happens, we should have a pretty good assessment concerning where the difficulty lies. It seems to me it doe not lie in the selling. With relation to the establishment of this new act, I would like to know what the international grading system is. If we in Canada cannot say that the system we are using is the type of system that would meet international standards, then it is the wrong system. If the minister can say there is no such thing as an international grading system, then it is about time we helped develop one. Whatever the international grading system is, we should participate in it and we should be marketing our grain on the basis of that grading system. Let us not talk
April 14, 1970

about the domestic market being in a different category, because we do not have a market of any size there.
If we buy a bag of flour from Czechoslovakia, when that bag arrives in Canada the protein and grade will be marked on it. All the particulars will be there. If we buy a bag of flour from Canada, we will be told that it is Canada's finest, the best procurable or that it is 100 per cent pure or something else which does not relate to grade. In Canada, we do not demand that there be any standard marked on the bag when the flour is for domestic consumption. The type of information marked on the bag is to the effect that it is general purpose flour or pastry flour. There is nothing which has any relation to grade, either internationally or domestically. There is no indication whether it is first or second grade, frozen, or has stones in it. Really, we are interested only in international grading. We must come to some understanding in respect of what that grade is, what our relationship to it is and what steps we should take in this regard.
In relation to this bill, the minister indicated that there will have to be more flexibility in our grading. He said the grading will be done by order in council. He said that new grades will be established by order in council when necessary, with certain limitations, provided certain other emergencies do not develop. I am not sure that is a bad thing. I am not sure it is good either, because I really do not know on what basis we are to establish these grades. I am of the opinion, however, that in Canada we have been overly protective of a system which may have become archaic many years ago. As everyone knows, we have developed recently a certain type of wheat with a low protein content but a very high yield. If we are to continue the production of wheat for feed grain purposes, then obviously it will be necessary to increase our production per acre in order to reduce our cost of production because that grain certainly will not sell at the same price as high protein wheat. So, I agree that there will need to be flexibility. But I believe there has been flexibility, although there has been reluctance on the part of the grain commissioners to accept that flexibility.
It was not too difficult for this particular minister, rightly or wrongly, to make the decision almost immediately that several new types of wheat would be released. This is really the first release in respect of a new 2221&-23
Canada Grain Act
type of wheat. There had been slight modifications over the years, but this is the first time in many years that a totally new type of wheat has been introduced into the grading system. So, there is flexibility.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMISSION, PROVISIONS RESPECTING GRADING, LICENCES, ELEVATORS, ETC.
speechtext: That is progress.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMISSION, PROVISIONS RESPECTING GRADING, LICENCES, ELEVATORS, ETC.
speechtext:
1 am not arguing that it is not progress. I think it is. But we had this flexibility under the old act, and also had a certain stability which in my opinion protected some farmers who were of the opinion-and they were certainly so advised-that the type and grade of wheat they were producing should not be reduced because the world was depending on No. 1 Northern high protein wheat. It seems that this really is not true. I hear that even Great Britain is buying wheat today on a straight protein basis from places like Argentina and Australia and apparently we are not able to meet that demand.
To be fair to the minister, I think he has done a number of other things, good and bad, which have had some effect on this situation. One of these has been the establishment of the block system. I think this system was established on the basis of the original concept of the terminal elevator. It was originally intended that certain grades could be established at inland and terminal elevators and delivered in both boat and trainload lots to the port terminals. However, over the years there has been a tendency for the country elevator to get rid of the type of grain that is most difficult to dispose of and at the same time fill up the elevator again because that is how they make their money. I can remember one Member of Parliament a few years age telling us that he was lucky enough to have loaded a car with flax seed or mustard seed and when this boxcar arrived at the coast it just happened that it was in the right position at the right time. He was able, therefore, to sell it for two or three times the amount he would have received otherwise because the buyer was there when the car was in position at the coast.
There has been considerable loading and shipping without any relationship to the ability to export or sell that commodity under a reasonable price structure. This has created some problems. I still do not understand why a transport controller has not been established. 1 realize the block system partly solves the difficulty in this regard, but we have had problems and I expect this fall and next year we will have problems again. I believe we will have these problems until someone is

April 14. 1970
Canada Grain Act
made totally responsible for the movement of the boxcars. I think that with a modern communications system we could probably connect that system with the boat shippings and other things involved in the movement of grain. When we do this we always are able to move a great deal of grain in this country. We seem to become involved in a good deal of difficulty when we let the railways handle the movement of grain themselves.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
The block system is applied mainly by the Wheat Board and the Board of Grain Commissioners to get the wheat into position, but we still need someone to move it along the track. This would seem to me to be the role of a transport commissioner who would have sufficient authority to oversee the movements and decide when the time is right for the sale program to be put into effect. Until we appoint a person who will be solely responsible for that operation, the block system will not function as well as it could, although it has already brought about a great improvement. The minister is to be congratulated for this.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMISSION, PROVISIONS RESPECTING GRADING, LICENCES, ELEVATORS, ETC.
speechtext: That authority is sought in the bill.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMISSION, PROVISIONS RESPECTING GRADING, LICENCES, ELEVATORS, ETC.
speechtext: That and a lot more.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMISSION, PROVISIONS RESPECTING GRADING, LICENCES, ELEVATORS, ETC.
speechtext:
The minister says that authority is sought in the bill. This raises a problem that I discussed with him personally concerning the individual car order book. The use of the individual car order book would mean that a person could order a car, have it delivered to his elevator and then load that car. He would have the right to do this. Probably this operation is not as practical as one could hope for, but nevertheless it was available. The block system may make it impossible for the farmer, if he is in the wrong protein grain area, to get loadings. This would be one of the responsibilities which I would give to a transport controller.
The new commission-and we will be interested to discuss this in the committee-will go some way toward the establishment of a relationship with the feed grain industry. A great many problems have arisen as a result of the fact that originally the feed grain industry was outside the jurisdiction of the Wheat Board. Sometimes officials of the Wheat Board come before the Agricultural Committee and say that barley is selling for 85 cents a bushel, and yet when they are questioned they admit

that it is actually selling for as low as 35 cents a bushel. Yet, it is the first figure that is presented to the minister. If I were the minister I would be very angry about this because he has to take responsibility in the House for those figures, and yet the members of the Board have admitted they knew these figures were not correct. They were not really sure what the exact figure was. So, by giving control of the feed grain industry to the grain commissioners, we will eliminate some of the major problems that are developing because a large portion of our sales in specific grades do not come within the control of the national agency and chaos is developing in that area.
I did not intend to speak for this long, but there are a couple of other comments I wish to make. They concern the relationship between these problems of production and sales, particularly export sales, and the operations of the producers themselves. There is probably no industry in Canada with which the government is more involved in an authoritative way than the agricultural industry. The involvement is not in money. It has not really made much of a contribution in monetary terms, but it has certainly made a great intrusion into the agricultural community through regulations. In the last few years the government has been saying to farmers: "Go out and expand. You cannot exist unless you have an economic farming unit". In western Canada, this means you need several sections of land and a very large expenditure for agricultural machinery. At the same time, the government said to the farmers: "It is not entirely our responsibility to sell your products". We lent a great deal of money to farmers to expand their farming units and to establish economic farm units. Then, we said to them: "We cannot sell your produce and we cannot do anything about the sales structure, so we will take your land out of production this year but we will pay you your cost of operation. We will not give you any money but we will pay you the cost of summerfallowing your land. We will not give you the money to pay the interest on your loans, nor will we give you any other consideration."
Tied to that proposal by the government is the new regulation which will affect every farmer who in the future will produce wheat and will sell that commodity to the Canadian Wheat Board under this grain legislation. We have told farmers what they can do and what they cannot do, but we have not given them much assistance. Now, we are establishing a whole new structure which will have a very
April 14. 1970

April 14, 1970
Canada Grain Act
which the international markets demand. As a result, farmers have not been able to cover their costs of production. I hope the bill will receive the type of consideration that will allow for an orderly transfer from the old legislation to the new, with provision for innovations that have been long overdue, to the advantage of all people concerned.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMISSION, PROVISIONS RESPECTING GRADING, LICENCES, ELEVATORS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on rising to take part in the discussion on Bill C-196 I do so with concern for the agricultural industry. Not since the 1930's have we seen farmers in western Canada, where the provisions of this bill will apply in particular, so anxious about what may be in store for them. We have seen the government offer western Canada $140 million, and then admit that only $100 million will be needed. But even following that, members of the government say, "We don't know how much of that will be used." The latest report by one Department of Agriculture official expresses his fear that farmers will not sufficiently reduce crops. Then comes this bill.
I listened to the speech made by the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters). He was eager to compliment the government for introducing this bill. But does this bill mention protein grading? It does not to any real extent. As recorded at page 5816 of yesterday's Hansard the hon. member for Sas-katoon-Biggar (Mr. Gleave) said protein grading should be provided under the terms of this bill, and the minister replied, "It will be."

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMISSION, PROVISIONS RESPECTING GRADING, LICENCES, ELEVATORS, ETC.
speechtext: It will be provided.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMISSION, PROVISIONS RESPECTING GRADING, LICENCES, ELEVATORS, ETC.
speechtext:
Again he says it will be provided. What else will be provided in this bill? Rigid, authoritative controls are also going to be provided through this bill. Elevators are to be licensed in four different ways. Now, grain dealers are to be licensed. Whether licensed dealers will be better than unlicensed ones I do not know. The bill practically limits the type of grain that one can produce because of the application of the block system.
We have seen the government attempt to limit farm production. Now, we see it attempting to bring about a protein grading system. I wish the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) and the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Lang) in charge of the Wheat Board could get together on their respective programs. If the Minister without Portfolio is going to bring about any wheat acreage reduction he is going to do so in the area that produces high protein wheat. If he is going to bring about any increase in wheat production,

it will be in the areas that produce low protein wheat.
Now, we see the Minister of Agriculture trying to establish that the reason our sales have gone off is that we have not really sold wheat under the protein content grading system. The idea of this system has caught fire in western Canada. A number of farm writers have said we should have adopted the protein grading system a long time ago, and that that is the reason why our sales have fallen. But let us not be misled in this House. Protein grading should have been adopted years ago but we did not lose all our markets because we did not adopt it, and now that we are going to adopt it this does not necessarily mean that buyers will be attracted to our door. We will still have to go out and sell our wheat.
If you have a product that is not moving and you cannot sell it at a discount, then you give your salesmen a little more incentive and maybe they will work a little harder to sell it. The President of the Winnipeg Grain Exchange has asked why a salesman should sell Canadian wheat. He has said such a man would make more money selling four cases of dog food to Japan than a full boatload of wheat. One of the brighter members of the agriculture committee replied that there were more people in Japan than dogs, and so there should be a better market for wheat there.
Is protein grading the real answer? I will go into that in detail. Will the program outlined by the minister in charge of the Wheat Board bring about a reduction in high grade protein wheat in western Canada? I think it will and I am going to outline why I think so and why that program will work directly contrary to this piece of legislation if, in fact, this piece of legislation brings about protein grading. What does protein content mean? I should like to read briefly from "Wheat Chemistry and Technology", page 31. Writing on protein content, the Author, Lawrence Zeleny states:
e (3:40 p.m.)
Protein content in wheat varies from about 6 per cent up to about 20 per cent, depending in part upon variety and class but more largely upon environmental factors during growth. Abundant rainfall during the period of kernel development usually results in low protein content, while dry conditions during that period favour high protein content.
Dry conditions produce high protein wheat. Is it going to pay farmers to summerfallow in low moisture areas where low yields are attained and where high protein wheat is produced? There will be no surplus wheat in
April 14. 1970

those areas. Any reduction in wheat acreage will not be because of the program introduced by the minister but because high protein wheat is not produced in surplus. This bill links the block system into the quota system and the regulation of the elevators is going to favour high protein wheat. This system does absolutely nothing for the producers of low protein wheat, other than to declare it feed wheat which will have to be sold to the licensed dealers. Whether those licensed dealers will have the right to transport it across provincial borders or all across Canada is not stated in the bill.
We have two pieces of legislation here which are diametrically opposed insofar as high protein areas are concerned. The area outside the high protein area is completely insignificant. Does that area always have to produce low protein wheat? The book "Wheat Chemistry and Technology" goes on to explain, in dealing with testing methods, that protein content can be considerably influenced by the availability of nitrogen in the soil and by the addition of nitrogen fertilizer. However, this bill does not mention what system of testing would be used.
How is the minister's program working? His own farm is in my riding. He attended a meeting there and discussed whether the LIFT program would help the farmers. I came along a few days later and attended a meeting with the same farmers. I asked them whether I explained the program any differently from the minister and they said that we had both explained it in the same way.

speechtext: It is all those bulletins we have been sending you.

speechtext:
The minister says it is all the bulletins he sent. But did the minister find that the farmers were accepting his program? I do not think he got any different reaction than I, when three farmers stood up and said they could take advantage of the program. At another meeting where 100 farmers attended, only four indicated their acceptance of the program and one of these told me afterwards that he shouldn't be counted as he will have to seed in order to live.
There is no general acceptance of the acreage reduction program that the Minister without Portfolio and the Minister of Agriculture introduced. It is definitely linked with this protein bill now before us and with the whole block delivery system. This bill and the block delivery system will eventually affect the quota system; the two go hand in hand.
Canada Grain Act
At a meeting in Brandon, Manitoba, attended by 700 farmers, only nine stood to indicate that they could take advantage of the quota. Surely, before this legislation is passed the man in charge of the Wheat Board, in consultation with the knowledgeable Minister of Agriculture who has long left the farm, will adjust the wheat acreage reduction program.
If the government has $100 million available for western Canadian farmers, should they not be bold enough to outline a plan that the farmers could take advantage of instead of one outlined and devised by academics? How can farmers in Saskatchewan take advantage of it when last year 18 million acres were under summerfallow and 16 million acres in wheat? How can they take any more land out of production? What effect will all that summerfallow have on the protein content next year when we are told that will be the basis upon which grain will be graded? The minister knows that you get low protein wheat but a higher yield under higher moisture conditions.
In an article appearing in the Calgary Herald on Saturday, April 11, 1970, an expert in the Department of Agriculture is quoted, under the heading "Farm Crop Cuts Not Yet Enough", as follows:
J. S. Carmichael, an economist with the agriculture department's markets information division, studied the prairie grain situation on the basis of the DBS survey. His report concludes that farmers need to reduce their planting intentions still more.
Canada already has 950 million bushels of hard red spring wheat on hand.
I do not believe Canada has that much wheat on hand, Mr. Speaker. This government, through the application of that acreage reduction program and this bill, are attempting to reduce the storage costs on wheat so that they will save the Treasury some money and not help the farmers one bit. That is why they kept storage space empty at the Lakehead for two months last winter, because storage costs the government one cent per bushel per month. This is the purpose of this bill.

Deafing with the last question first, I feel that if we were to revert to a policy of selling on a basis of guaranteed protein not only would it necessitate-
This is the point on which the minister said "not so", and I want to emphasize that:
-a complete revamping of our handling and selling systems but I cannot see where we would benefit by it. We have explored this with many buyers Of the world and we find that they are not prepared to pay a premium although they would like to have it guaranteed. [DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
Mr. McNamara is the chairman of the Canadian Wheat Board, so I suppose he is in disfavour. We have to admit he is one of the most able men in the trade. He is over 70 years old and is still kept on by the government, not because of his youth or flexibility but because of his knowledge. He said we shall have to revamp our whole handling system. This bill is designed to revamp it and to reduce the quantity of wheat held in commercial storage, so that the government can get out from under the provisions of the Temporary Wheat Reserves Act of 1956. We are geared to a bulk handling system, and I still think it is the most efficient system-[DOT]
The chairman of the Wheat Board is saying that if we adopt a protein grading system we must change our handling system. He makes that very clear, from my reading of the committee proceedings. He further says that this new method of protein grading and the changes in our handling system will entail mixing at the terminal; but the minister did not say anything about that in his speech. This bill is full of verbiage; the wraps have not even been taken off it and we do not know the minister's full intention. Answering an earlier question he said, yes, that it will
[Mr. Olson.1
include provisions relating to protein grading. I do not know whether the question was asked of him with respect to mixing in terminals.

speechtext: Certainly, it will have to provide for the mixing at terminals. Mr. McNamara has something to say about mixing at terminals. Mr. McNamara went on to say this, as reported at page 1246 of Minutes of Proceedings and Evidence No. 32 of the Standing Committee on Agriculture:
I am very much opposed to terminal mixing. I know that there is a wide school of thought on this, and I can see that in some of the lower feeding grades, commercial grades, and so on, modifications are required, but I think, personally-and I am not
April 14, 1970

speaking necessarily for my Board on this; because I have held these views for years-that for us to have terminal mixing of our higher grades would result in a much lower quality of product going into the foreign markets.
What he says about foreign markets is pretty clear. He goes on to say:
And one thing we need to maintain at this time is the quality of our exports. Recently there was a case in Japan where the Americans got into a lot of serious trouble. This was mainly because of terminal mixing at the west-coast ports. The quality was not satisfactory. They had to take steps to correct it. speechtext:
Now, he says it will take place under the supervision of the Board of Grain Commissioners. Did Mr. McNamara ever believe it would take place under no supervision. He fully believed it would be supervised.
We are told that by revamping our grading and handling systems we may possibly sell more wheat. We may, but not necessarily. In this connection, I have raised questions before the Standing Committee on Agriculture repeatedly over the past ten years. May I refer to Minutes of Proceedings and Evidence No. 41 of the Standing Committee on Agriculture. At page 1586 Mr. Treleaven of the Canadian Wheat Board is answering questions about British sales and why sales have dropped off to Europe and Great Britain. He says this:
... there are two or three factors that enter into a decrease in our total sales volume to the United Kingdom.
Mr. McNamara has touched on one and that is the fact of the changes in milling technology. This is a very, very sophisticated milling country, changes in milling technology have allowed them to use less of the strong wheats-[DOT]
I emphasize the word "strong" because a strong wheat is spoken of when people mean high protein wheat. I continue:
__in their grist and still get an acceptable loaf of
bread. So there has been in general a decrease in the proportion of high quality strong wheats that they have bought.
He goes on to say:
Today more and more of that trade is going by trans-shipment from northern European ports- through Rotterdam, Antwerp, and Amsterdam.
Canada Grain Act
He also said that the United Kingdom is buying wheat from central European countries, including Spain, and that they are melding all this wheat into a grist, still using Canadian wheat as the basis, to get the cheapest commodity they can and still produce an acceptable loaf of bread. Although I accept the idea behind protein rating, I do not see that it will bring about gigantic increases in our sales. It could be that the regulatory controls envisaged in this bill and the increased red tape will mean that farmers will obtain less cash for the same amount of work.
The government is saying to western agriculture, and to Canadian agriculture in general, "Please take your reserve land out of production." If Canadian farmers could only produce enough feed grain, we could produce enough hogs, cattle and poultry to supply the needs of this country. Last year, 7 per cent of the beef consumed in Canada was imported; last year we imported 60 million pounds of pork, which is about 400,000 hogs. If we could use our surplus grain profitably, we would not need to import poultry, eggs and all the rest of it. We would not need to import over $10 million worth of poultry and over $20 million worth of eggs. That sounds like a lot of eggs.

speechtext:
The minister talks about
exports. True, we exported quite a bit of beef and pork, but we could export more. We should not necessarily cut back our production. The farmers are looking for hope; they are looking for leadership and do not want to be told, "Cut back, and we will give you $6 an acre to quit farming certain land." That $6 per acre would not even pay the interest on the money that is tied up. Has the minister ever said that he intends to introduce a moratorium on Farm Credit Corporation loans or on loans used for the purpose of buying machinery from farm machinery companies? Some companies are foreclosing. I ask the minister whether he would not look into the operations of the farm machinery companies and whether he would not be willing to use, if necessary, the recommendations in the Barber Commission as a means of curbing the activities of some farm machinery companies. But no; we have two ministers in this area, under the old maxim of divide and rule. The Prime Minister went out to Winnipeg some time ago and said, "Why should I sell your wheat?" He did not sell it, but made two

April 14, 1970
Canada Grain Act
ministers responsible for agricultural matters. One of those ministers has introduced a program that is unacceptable. The western farmers would like to be able to accept it. Last week I asked the minister in charge of the Wheat Board if he would accept a change in the guaranteed eight bushel quota. Why could it not be transferable to barley or some other crop?
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
Although 75 per cent of the farmers in western Canada do not have a surplus of wheat, they may have 50 per cent of their land in summerfallow. They may have a quota. They are going to seed wheat this year because the eight bushel quota is the only guarantee they are given. The sad thing about most of that area is that the northern part and along the foothills, which produces the low protein wheat, will not be covered by this bill. We see confusion at its best.
The minister, who may well have been on the farm at one time, happily left the farm. He has had the farm problems dumped in his lap and has now come up with an economic trick that is causing a nightmare throughout western Canada. The farmers are attending meetings, 700 farmers in Brandon, 12,000 in Regina, 6,000 in Saskatoon-

right that someone knowledgeable should go along on the trip.
What are the facts with regard to protein grading of wheat and the grading of wheat in other countries? Approximately 82 per cent of the wheat produced in Australia is low protein. Is the wheat acreage being cut back in that country? The 1970 figure shows that Australia has not cut back one bit. I see the minister shaking his head. I suggest that he read the report on wheat marketing prepared by Mr. Hudson for the Economic Council of Canada.
What about the United States? That country is supposed to be selling wheat according to protein content. According to the report of the agriculture committee the United States is not doing too well with mixing at the terminals, and has got into trouble with Japan. Is that country cutting back on wheat acreage? They are not cutting back at all. In fact, the northern states, Montana and the Dakotas, have been encouraged to increase their wheat acreage because of Canada's action. What is the net result? Canada is the only country of the five major wheat exporting countries that has said, we quit. Canada is the only country to take that negative approach. The minister shakes his head. He can make his own speech later if he likes. Canada has acted negatively and continues to do so. This bill may or may not do much for us. I am not prepared to judge it as good or bad until I have had an opportunity to examine it fully in committee.
There is no protein grading. Is it the French grading system we are to adopt? Are we going to adopt the Russian system? That country grades on the basis of protein to some extent. Are there two levels of cellulose and protein content that are going to be judged? We are not given this information. Will we be in a better competitive position with France? It is France that seems to be undercutting the price in the International Grains arrangement. I talked to the former minister in charge of the Wheat Board. I asked him whether Canada had notified the French government that Canada was anxious because of their price-cutting, but he said we had not done so. It was left up to the Wheat Board. He informed me the International Grains Arrangement countries were going to be meeting somewhere at some time. That is not good enough.
Farmers in western Canada have never wanted subsidies or handouts. They want a chance to produce. They have proven that
April 14, 1970

they are very efficient, because they have gotten along with less subsidies than the farmers of any other country of the world. Western farmers want the government, the Wheat Board and the Board of Grain Commissioners to sell their product. If these agencies are unable to sell it, the farmers would like at least an honest effort to be made. This government has failed to do that. The Prime Minister in a shrugging, fanciful way said in Winnipeg, "Why should I sell your wheat?"
As far back as 1935, the Wheat Board was the responsibility of the government. The Wheat Board officials were appointed by the government and were therefore the direct responsibility of that minister of the crown who had nothing else to do but look after the Wheat Board and encourage the farmers on to greater heights. He has not done a good job. That minister, too, has accepted a negative line of thinking. The minister says, if we cannot sell it, then we had better not produce it. We are the only country in the world to adopt this attitude. The United States cut back wheat production in an orderly way 20 years ago, but they have not cut back any more in the last couple of years. The minister holds out a report which purports to say otherwise. In the last two years in particular, the United States has not cut back wheat acreage.
This program will bring about a wheat acreage reduction in the areas producing high protein wheat. While selling and grading on the basis of protein content may be used as a scapegoat by the government to show why we have lost sales. I say we have lost sales because we have not paid enough attention to the selling angle. We were ready to accept the negative approach that we should curtail production.
The government stated that they were prepared to give to the western farmers $140 million and then said, knowingly, that the figure amount used would be $100 million. In their hearts, they know that only $30 million or $40 million can possibly be accepted by these farmers, even with the best conditions in western Canada. Is the government prepared to adjust its program so that the farmers can take advantage of the $100 million they reportedly are prepared to give them? Neither minister is prepared to adjust his program. Both ministers know that under the program farmers cannot accept more than $30 million or $40 million. The minister shakes his head. He knows better because he has been meeting the same farmers as I have and has been hearing the same results. The Minis-
Canada Grain Act

These reports show there will be a voluntary wheat acreage reduction by the farmers of 26 per cent and a 5 per cent increase in summerfallow. Under the government's program, the farmers will only be paid on the 5 per cent increase in summerfallow. Five per cent of $100 million is $5 million. I was over generous when I said $30 million or $40 million.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on Bill C-196 I would be the first to say that I am in general agreement with the aims of this bill, which is to revamp the Canada Grain Act, something that has stood for over 40 years. It is significant, in view of the rapidity of change in our modem world, that the Canada Grains Act is only now being revamped, and this indicates that the original act was either exceptionally good or that changes in our grading system have not occurred to a marked extent.
This revamping of our grading system, mainly in the field as I understand it of protein grading of wheat, is at least five years overdue. This bill brings into sharp focus the case for the government passing the standards bill that is now on the Order Paper. Govern-

April 14, 1970
Canada Grain Act
ment proponents of the standards bill indicate that voluntary standardization is not enough, that it is much too slow to be effective in a modern world.	On
the other hand, grading regulations have been entirely under government control and have not been changed for 40 years. This seems to indicate that there is no real evidence that governments move particularly fast when they are called upon to review regulations in a particular industry. Indeed, the slowness of the government in dealing with the Canada Grains Act would be a good indication that the standards bill will result in a similar slow down of changes in standards rather than accelerate them.
The indications for change in this bill have been brought about mainly by the need for protein grading in our export sales of wheat. Knowledgeable people to whom I have talked in the grain industry do not feel that protein grading will in itself increase sales of wheat in the export markets, but that unless this is carried forward we will be unable to maintain even our diminishing percentage of the world market. We in Canada are particularly dependent on the export of wheat to support the basic plank in the western grain economy. This income has in general a very marked .effect on total income not only in western Canada but in the whole of Canada. Indeed, the export of western resources such as wheat, meat, oil seeds, oil and gas, minerals and forest products are the means whereby Canada is able to have a standard of living second only to that of the United States.
At the present time various factors are at work within the Canadian government structure that seem to be doing their best to antagonize our customers abroad. At the same time we are involving ourselves in an extremely heavy welfare-orientated government program; the government is proposing to cut down investment level by implementing its white paper on taxation; and it is attempting to create a bilingual political and economic system. All of this makes us a less competitive nation in the markets of the world. Recently we began to engage in curtailing foreign investment in our resources.
Protein grading of wheat may well be used as the scapegoat for all our ills and lack of export sales. In fact, though important, it has been only one of the many hard facts we have to face. For example, more countries of the world are becoming self-sufficient at this time in cereal grain production, and competition is becoming greater and more intense.

Just three years ago it was suggested that Canada could grow all the wheat it could, for which a ready market would be found. The present state of our grain sales indicate that this is not so.
In the report of the Economic Council of Canada the commissioner pointed out that:
Canada has achieved a rate erf growth of labour productivity and agriculture well above that recorded in other sectors of the economy, and I'll roughly compare comparable dimensions to the rate of growth of agricultural labour productivity in the United States. However, the substantial disparity between the two countries in the absolute level of agricultural labour productivity has widened significantly. Mechanization and yield technology have contributed in nearly equal proportions to growth in the United States. In contrast, Canada has advanced in the area of mechanization but not kept pace in yield technology.
This would indicate that merely researching the guaranteed protein content is not the panacea when we consider the marketing problems of western Canadian wheat. It also indicates that we should be having a second look at the main factors that influence the productivity of the Canadian farmer. Family farms handed down from generation to generation must be virtually bought back from the government. Payment of estate and capital gains taxes and increased tax on the middle income group mitigate against easy acquisition of Canadian farms by a new farming generation.
Canada's percentage of the grain market has dropped from 24 per cent to 19 per cent in recent years and strenuous efforts will be needed to regain this share. Nevertheless, so far as this bill is concerned, protein grading should be introduced without too much dislocation of our markets in the world.
The complexity of marketing problems and changes that might have to be necessitated in wheat grading are indicated by a recent study of the Canadian-American Committee of the National Planning Association and the Private Planning Association of Canada. One of the commission members, Mr. Arden Bur-bridge of North Dakota, suggested that our grading system may have discriminated against developing countries that could have been major customers of ours by setting champagne standards for customers with beer budgets. He is quoted in today's issue of the Globe and Mail, April 14, as follows:
These undeveloped countries have a need expressed more in terms of tons of wholesome nutrients without great concern for fine points of quality (such as bread colour, low volume and baking time).
April 14, 1970

With limited foreign exchange, it would seem that they would prefer to be able to negotiate price to take advantage of their lower quality demands.
Thus, by holding a fixed, rigid price, the exporting countries discriminate against our greatest potential future growth market.
He also suggested that unrealistic demands for high quality wheat prevent the switch to higher yielding semi-dwarf varieties whose quality, while slightly lower, would be adequate for this important market. The switch to protein marketing will have quite far-reaching and serious consequences on the pattern of grain growing in western Canada. For many years the Palliser triangle has been the area of Canada which usually produced the high protein grain that would bring a premium in world markets and which also contained the gluten and baking qualities necessary to meet the requirements of markets in Europe and Japan.
The whole parkland area outside the Palliser Triangle poses a problem in that it has been growing wheat for many years and the farm economy is geared substantial to wheat growing. If this area were not able to produce high protein saleable wheat, and if the discount on what they produced was too low then this whole area would be economically disadvantaged. However, should markets remain available in countries where low protein wheat is acceptable, then it may well continue its role as a wheat growing area in western Canada.
[DOT] (4:20 pm.)
Also there seems to be substantial evidence that the protein level of wheat can be increased by judicious application of nitrogen so that in most years, even with the present varieties of wheat, substantial quantities of high protein wheat can be produced in parkland areas. It would seem possible that high yielding protein wheat can be developed for this parkland area and research would be indicated in this field. Otherwise, if there should have to be a cessation of wheat growing in much of the parkland areas of western Canada, there would be great economic dislocation and hardship. With this in mind, I should like to point out the possibility, that with the United States using protein grading right at the farmer's bin, this would seem to be much more fair than attempting to have a particular area designation.
There is one important aspect of this bill in respect of which I reserve judgment, and that is that all changes in grading are at the whim 22218-24!
Canada Grain Act
of the Governor in Council. This means that in the future any changes in the grading system can be made with simple disregard for Parliament. It has been 40 years since the Canada Grains Act has been amended. It would seem to have been a reasonable success, and it has remained under the control of Parliament. This usurption of power is becoming an everyday occurrence on the part of this government. It would appear they consider that in future all changes in the grading of grain should not be in the hands of Parliament but only in the hands of the Governor in Council.
The minister has stated it is necessary to move quickly, so power must be retained within the government at all times. There have been no major changes in the grain act for 40 years and it has always been the government's prerogative to introduce legislation at any time to make changes. Protein grading should have been instituted some years ago, yet the government has shown that it has not been worried about this problem. So far at least, changes in grading should be made only after reasonable consultation with the producer and marketing groups, and finally with elected representatives in the House of Commons.
Recent changes in the acreage quota by order in council leave much to be desired. Just recently we had operation LIFT proposed by the minister, which seems to have been introduced after very little consultation with producer groups. Under the LIFT program, the minister hoped that no wheat would be grown in western Canada during the coming year. To have followed up the minister's idea in its entirety would have been a disastrous economic move for the grain farmers and die western economy in general. Fortunately, the farmers seem to have more sense than the Minister and seem to be thinking about a modest reduction to approximately 15 million acres of wheat. This seems likely all that can be done in one year.
The minister in charge of the Wheat Board has indicated that he expects the Wheat Board will only buy from the producers somewhere in the neighbourhood of 250 million to 300 million bushels of wheat based on an eight bushel quota. Obviously, he further expected that the normal intake of about 450 million bushels of wheat from a crop year would be reduced.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. The hon. member referred to

April 14, 1970
Canada Grain Act
figures concerning the amount of wheat expected to be produced next year by the farmers, as though those figures had been given by me at some time. These figures are completely in error. subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMISSION, PROVISIONS RESPECTING GRADING, LICENCES, ELEVATORS, ETC.
speechtext:
I am glad the minister made that statement, because no matter how you figure this, on the basis of only eight bushels per specified acre it does not work out. Many farmers will not have the wheat to fill their acreage quotas unless they grow wheat. It does not seem reasonable that the Wheat Board will be obligated to take from the producers as a whole more than 300 million bushels of wheat. If every farmer had wheat to fulfil the eight bushels per authorized acre quota, then we could expect to have 400 million bushels of wheat. I suggest there will not be anything like this distribution of wheat.
In other words, through operation LIFT, the minister is asking that grain farmers reduce their deliveries by 100 million to 150 million bushels unless there is an increase in the amount specified for delivery to much above eight bushels per acre, and he has not indicated to my satisfaction that he intends to do that. What he proposes will help out the storage position of the Wheat Board, but I would submit that at this time it is too much to ask the grain farmer to reduce deliveries by 100 million to 150 million bushels based on the eight bushel allocated quota. With this in mind, I have considerable reservation about grading being entirely the prerogative of the Governor in Council, and I would hope that this phase will be very closely examined in the committee.
Another important feature is the block system of moving all grain. This seems to have considerable advantages but has shown weaknesses in the movement of flax and rape-seed into export positions during the past year. There is no doubt that during this last fall flax and rapeseed sales were lost because oilseeds were not in position. One of the reasons seems to be that the block system is not too helpful in moving these relatively small quantities of grain into forward positions at all desirable times.

As far as the minister's comment on the checkoff for research purposes is concerned, I will only say at this time that this should be carefully examined by the committee and that some recommendations should be brought forward. This is an exceptionally complex bill which involves very difficult phases of the Canadian grain trade. No doubt committee hearings will throw a great deal more light on the functions of this act.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMISSION, PROVISIONS RESPECTING GRADING, LICENCES, ELEVATORS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, other hon. members of this party and other parties in opposition have directed their attention to some of the intrinsic difficulties in the bill and have made a very convincing case why it is so essential that this bill be subjected to the closest possible scrutiny of the committee, particularly as to its objects. I have other objections which I should like to put before the House at this time. I am not going to infringe upon the rules, but in order to make my case I must say that the objectives of the bill, as set out in large part in clause 11, constitute such a grave infringement of the traditional restrictions on the kind of power given to the government it taints the whole bill and justifies a complete review.
What are the objects of the proposed Canadian Grain Commission which presumably will administer the act. They are set out in clause 11 of the bill which reads in part as follows:
Subject to this Act and any direction to the Commission issued from time to time under this Act by the Governor in Council or the Minister, the Commission shall establish and maintain standards of quality for Canadian grain and regulate and supervise grain handling in Canada-
This is the first part in respect of which I take grievous exception. To begin with, as I read this clause, the commission and the Governor in Council can extend these objectives beyond grain, as defined by Parliament in Part I, to include for example any seed. The clause places two duties upon the commission, each one to achieve a purpose. The clause spells out the means by which the commission is to achieve those purposes. The first purpose is to ensure maximum acceptance of Canadian grain as a commodity of dependable quality in domestic and export markets. This purpose is to be achieved by maintaining standards and quality for Canadian grain.
The second purpose is to ensure an efficient grain handling system, which is to be achieved by regulation and supervision of grain handling in Canada.
April 14. 1970



[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
This definition of purposes and means appears to be qualified in two ways. The definition is made subject to this act and, more important, to any directions to the Commission issued from time to time under this act by the Governor in Council or the minister, as I have read from proposed clause 11. These restrictions cannot be understood unless some of the excess verbiage is cleared away. The words "subject to this act" are meaningless. In the first place, clause 11 will be part of the act itself and can hardly be subject to itself. In the second place, the words "subject to", as here used, are analogous to "not inconsistent with this act". Mr. Driedger, a one-time eminent civil servant, a deputy minister and now a lecturer of law, in an authoritative text on this subject states:
Sometimes authority is conferred to make regulations not inconsistent with the act. These words are unnecessary. Even in their absence it would not be permissible to make regulations contrary to or inconsistent with the act itself.
In other words, under the rules of statutory interpretation, the duties of the Commission as expressed in clause 11 must be carried out by the Commission in a manner that does not violate the specific provisions enacted by Parliament elsewhere in the act. We are then left with the words "subject to.. .any direction to the Commission issued from time to time under this act by the Governor in Council or the minister." These words are indeed restrictive on the Commission in its duty to carry out the two objects expressed in clause 11; but they constitute a delegation of power to the Governor in Council and to the minister this is unrestricted and unconditional in terms and confined only by the title of the bill. Presumably it will be argued in rebuttal that these words are descriptive; that is, they relate to powers elsewhere delegated in the bill to the Governor in Council and to the minister. But this argument cannot be supported. In the first place, if the phrase is only descriptive of delegated powers defined in other parts of the bill, why are the words "under this act" used?
Again, it is my submission that the Canadian Wheat Board or the Commission, as the case may be, is restricted to dispose of overages as directed by the Governor in Council. This is not a provision that affects the objects of the Commission. There is indeed no need to refer to it in clause 11. The next delegation of power is in clause 78, which empowers the minister to review the Commission's refusal or revocation of an elevator or grain dealer
Canada Grain Act
licence and to direct the Commission to issue or reinstate a licence. This is an appeal procedure and does not run counter to the objects expressed in clause 11. I consider this to be a very serious breach of the type of parliamentary condition which should be laid down when a minister is permitted to sit in judgment and render a decision which affects the rights and liberties of the people of Canada, including those to whom a licence has been issued by the commission. The commission is given further authority with regard to the issuing of licences and the conditional revoking of licences. Then, the bill provides that from that commission there can be appeal to a political person or tribunal, without the protections which we in this country want to maintain.
I have not established this argument to the extent I might have, but I should like to make plain that I object to this granting of authority to the minister to sit as a court of appeal upon decisions of a commission. More than ever, I object to the fact that clause 11 is an unlimited, uncontrolled and improper delegation of power to the Governor in Council and the minister to make laws for any purpose they may see fit pertaining to seeds. This government has become a genius in giving to itself large chunks of power by the writing of regulations and the passage of orders in council. I have continuously objected to this procedure. I think some day the country will wake up to the fact that it has made a very serious error in giving away to a group of people, such as any cabinet or government, the right to do some of the things we have given them the right to do. But this bill would go further. In effect it would authorize the Governor in Council to legislate in respect of objects beyond those included in the bill. This is what we are doing. Apparently we are doing this quite willingly. The government backbenchers are quite happy about it. I am not. I think this is something we should regard far more seriously.
I prepared a reasoned amendment which under normal circumstances I would have moved. However, for reasons I shall set out, I do not intend to move this amendment at this time. This amendment would have been to the effect that this bill be not procedeed with now as it conflicts with the principle of this House that this House will not give the government or a minister of the government legislative power to amend or define the purposes and provisions of an Act of this Parliament or the objects of a body created by that

April 14. 1970
Canada Grain Act
Act. For other reasons, I am now of the opinion that I should object to the bill generally and therefore it becomes unnecessary for me to move this amendment. These other reasons, stated succinctly, are the following. This is a money bill. As there must be, there appears on the first page of the printed bill the recommendation. His Excellency the Governor General has recommended to the House of Commons the present measure respecting grain because it involves the expenditure and appropriation of money.
Over the last few days, we in the opposition have been involved in a rather traumatic experience with regard to the opportunities which exist for the officials of this House to scrutinize and call to the attention of the House what, in their opinion, are the errors of omission and commission of the government, of government departments, of government tribunals and of Crown corporations in connection with the expenditure of money which has been voted by this House. I am referring specifically to the Auditor General. Because of the attitude taken by this government, particularly by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) and the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Macdonald), I take strong exception to this House granting the right to this government to appropriate money unless and until this particular situation has been clarified. For that reason, speaking for myself, I am not prepared to give approval to the passage of this legislation. I shall set out as clearly and in as short a fashion as possible, my reasons for this attitude.
What is to be the fate of the Auditor General, whoever he may be, when he scrutinizes the expenditures made under the Provisions of this bill? When I refer to these expenditures I have in mind the enormous powers I have cited which give the government the right to set forth completely any objects unrelated to the proposals in the bill. What is to be the fate of that money? To what extent are we in this House, who have a duty here as the servants of the people who have elected us, to have an opportunity to conduct a searching and close examination of these expenditures? I submit that what has taken place constitutes a valid reason for me to say to the government that it cannot have these powers until it clarifies precisely where it stands on this situation. If the government introduces a money bill, it must be prepared to indicate at this time, in my view, that a

clear and definite responsibility rests upon it with regard to the audit of the money which will be granted.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
Let me go over this briefly. The President of the Privy Council (Mr. Macdonald), in a television interview not so long ago, stated:
We recognize the fact that it's his responsibility to audit the accounts and to account for the manner in which the funds have been expended. We don't think it's his responsibility to give legal opinions with regard to the manner of carrying out the policies and, in particular, we don't regard it as being his responsibility to criticize the underlying policy involved in certain decisions.

With respect to this revision of the Canada Grain Act, Mr. Speaker, my remarks will be brief because many of the problems have already been covered by my colleagues.
I want to serve notice on the government that the proposed revision of the Canada Grain Act in Bill C-196, referred to as an act respecting grain, is not going to be a panacea for the present economic problems facing western Canadian grain farmers. Neither is operation LIFT, or what our farmers refer to as the Fanners' Income Reduction Plan, going to be the answer, as both the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) and the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Lang) responsible for the Wheat Board very well know.
In my opinion the emphasis being placed both on this legislation and on operation LIFT is greatly overrated, and is basically an admission of the government's failure to sell wheat. There is no doubt that the Canada Grain Act, first developed in 1930, needs updating. The legislation at that time was enacted for the protection of the producers, and set standards for Canadian wheat, which not only was recognized as the best bread wheat in the world but because of the grading system could be sold anywhere in the world by sample.
Although most of our wheat will still be sold by sample, it has become apparent that a new grading system is needed to satisfy some of our better customers as to the protein content of the grain offered. This is particularly so in West Germany, Japan and Britain, where new baking techniques are being used. In my study of the bill I failed to find any
Canada Grain Act
reference to protein grading, but as explained by the minister in his opening statement authority is provided whereby grades may be changed at any time by Order in Council. In fact, it is this provision giving the minister authority to make changes, allocate boxcars and generally direct the movement of different kinds and grades of grain to the terminals, that I find a little disturbing. Certainly, the government will be involved in the grain business, whether the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) would like to shrug off the responsibility or not.
The bill provides that the grains Commission will have authority to licence all grain handling facilities, including feed mills, to regulate and supervise grain handling in Canada, as well as to establish and maintain standards of quality for Canadian grain, subject to directions issued to the commission from time to time by the Governor in Council, or the minister. The protein grading of wheat brings up some very interesting questions. I believe that I am right in saying that sales of wheat made in the past to the Communist countries have been in the lower bread grades of No. 3 and No. 4 Northern. Is it possible that in the future these countries will want to buy their grain on a protein basis?
I hope that in changing the grading system, and re-arranging our transportation and grain handling facilities, it will not be forgotten that practically all areas of western Canada must grow wheat as part of their crop rotation, and all grades will be needed as part of our export pattern. This is a point that was brought out last night by my colleague from Mackenzie when he opened this debate, because he comes from an area of western Canada where approximately 35 per cent of the farmers may not be able to sell their wheat under a protein grading system.

Mr. Speaker, it is with pleasure that I express my humble views on the legislative proposal presented today by the hon. member for Surrey (Mr. Mather).
In spite of the many interesting explanations he has just given us, I must say honestly that I am against this bill for the following reasons.
First, without being a strong supporter of the status quo in all fields, I suggest that we must maintain it for some time with regard to this matter.
As a matter of fact, since I was elected to the House in 1965, the problem of lobbyists who come to see members of the Commons or the Senate in both chambers or in the committees, is not a very serious one. In my view, there is no such problem.
Even if I am opposed to this bill, this does not mean that the arguments submitted by the hon. member for Surrey are not valid ones. On the contrary, he expressed himself in a sober and sincere manner; he was well documented to show the validity of his assertions. However, I wish to come back to a principle which I have often voiced in the House and which is dear to me: there is no perfect institution on this planet. In fact, we must always try to improve, to progress with the flow of the best evolutionary process, which is

April 14. 1970
Lobbying Control Act
an attitude becoming more and more fashionable in all fields. Furthermore, I feel that any modern man must recognize this principle and arrange his life in keeping with this evolution.
As pressures made in Canada by certain groups of people who engage in lobbying, as it is usually called, are linked to the nature of parliamentary institutions, I feel that we must consider the possibility of improving in a general and global way these parliamentary institutions as well as this lobbying.
That is why when we talk about improving our parliamentary institutions-be it the operation of the House of Commons, of the committees, of the Senate or our relations with the public-I suggest that a task force made up of independent, competent and free men should first make a thorough study of the situation.
As recommended by the member for Surrey, we must apply our energies to improve certain things in order to ensure the proper operation of the government and of our judiciary system.
If each of us tries to improve such or such an aspect of our institutions, as the member for Surrey is doing today with respect to lobbying, next another member will ask for a reform of the international organization of the House, and later another member or group of members will make representations regarding the working conditions of members of Parliament and Senators.
With all due respect to the House, I think this procedure is too haphazard. It is a little like a doctor trying to cure an organic disease which causes headaches by ordering his patient to take aspirin only. It might relieve the patient but it would not eliminate the cause of the disease. That is why I am convinced that for the moment it is better to maintain the status quo.
In my opinion, the House has more important duties. It would be more desirable to maintain the status quo until experts have summarized our needs and tried to determine how we can improve our parliamentary institutions of which we can be proud. The principles they stand for remain but parliamentary institutions could be made better, at least as far as the application of these principles is concerned.
When I refer to the status quo, I am thinking about lobbying, the action of lobbyists who try to influence the work of the govern-

ment or even that of members of the judiciary. I think that it would be advisable to ask ourselves what our present institutions are worth and to make the necessary distinctions.
Allow me to quote Standing Order 114 concerning the role of parliamentary agents. I think, as stated by the mover of the bill, that the role of the parliamentary agents can be related to that of lobbyists who wish to influence Parliament in one way or another when a piece of legislation has to be passed.
The Standing Order in question reads as follows:
(1)	No person shall act as parliamentary agent conducting proceedings before the House of Commons or its committees without the express sanction and authority of Mr. Speaker, and all such agents shall be personally responsible to the House and to Mr. Speaker, for the observance of the rules, orders and practice of Parliament and rules prescribed by Mr. Speaker, and also for the payment of all fees and charges.
(2)	A list of such persons shall be kept by the Chief Clerk of Private Bills and a copy filed with the Clerk of the House.
(3)	No person shall be allowed to be registered as a parliamentary agent during any session unless he has paid a fee of twenty-five dollars for such session and is actually employed in promoting or opposing some private bill or petition pending in Parliament during that session.
Standing Order 115 sets out what the parliamentary agents are liable to if they wilfully act in violation of the rules. This order reads partly as follows:
-shall be liable to an absolute or tempory prohibition to practice as a parliamentary agent, at the pleasure of Mr. Speaker; provided that upon the application of such agent, Mr. Speaker shall state in writing the ground for such prohibition.

Lobbying Control Act Everyone here is aware that for many reasons, a month or two after the beginning of the session, or toward the end of a session, it may be in the public interest that lobbyists come to make representations to their member of Parliament. As for the penalty; the bill provides as follows:
-five hundred dollars or imprisonment for three months, or both fine and imprisonment.
I am still wondering why the hon. member imagines that anything so serious can take place in this field as to call for a $500 fine or imprisonment for three months or both. Furthermore, he refers to the case of a Canadian citizen, remunerated or not. What difference does it make whether a Canadian citizen, to act in this capacity, is remunerated or not? If someone has lobbying to do, it can be presumed that he will not be remunerated. However, when a company or a group has representatives lobbying on its behalf, we all know that remuneration is normal.
What about groups such as the Catholic Farmers' Union in eastern Canada-the area where I come from-which having to make representations to the Canadian legislators, would be subject to these rules, whatever remuneration is paid to its representatives, or even whether or not it is represented.
There are very important pressure groups in Canada. The hon. member for Surrey (Mr. Mather) has already indicated it to the House.
