This afternoon I went to the Parliamentary Library to look up some works on the subject of lobbying. It would astonish hon. members to know that there are in the Parliamentary Library about 40 books on the subject of lobbying. There is a shelf of these books as long as the arm of the hon. member for Surrey, and he is a tall fellow. Practically without exception all these books were written in the United States, because that is where lobbying has developed to a very high science, a much higher science than we find here. In the United States, particularly in respect of committees, there is very intense lobbying.
Here the procedure is much simpler than in the United States Congress. Lobbying in the United States has developed to a very fine art compared with lobbying in Canada or even in

Great Britain. One reason, of course, is that the United States is a large country with great riches and groups of people, companies and organizations are very interested in the influence they can bring to bear on legislation.
I brought into the House of Commons this afternoon a text entitled "Co-operative Lobbying-The Power of Pressure" by Donald R. Hall. This is a very recent book on the subject of lobbying in the United States. It is Very interesting to read a paragraph or two concerning what this man has to say about the practice in the United States. He says:
The lobbyist is both artist and scientist, a person of whom high standards are demanded. His education and income compare favourably with those of other white-collar professionals in America. The elite among lobbyists are public figures, socially acceptable in high places, often the confidants of Presidents and other high officials.
There is a little paragraph in which he tells about one of these individuals. I know it would be of interest to the House if I were to pinpoint exactly what he means when he refers to this type of person. I read from page 8 of the text:
The most "in" lobbyist in Washington these days is a highly social specimen. Tall, white-maned, mild-mannered Dale Miller is a genuine son-of-a-lobbyist whose father got Lyndon Johnson his first Washington job as secretary to a Congressman. He has been the President's friend for 30 years.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMISSION, PROVISIONS RESPECTING GRADING, LICENCES, ELEVATORS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the debate on Bill C-196, an act respecting grain, ended at five o'clock to allow for private members' hour I was commenting on the remarks made previously by the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Korchinski) who was seriously concerned about a large number of our western wheat farmers who might find themselves in a low protein area if proposals in the bill are brought into effect. He had a very valid point
Canada Grain Act
and I would like an explanation from the minister as to how these farmers would be treated if they should be limited to the sale of wheat growing in those areas and were not able to conform to the level of proteins set forth in any of the new grading systems.
Any government decision to phase out wheat in certain areas for some mythical supply management theory would be repugnant to the average western farmer who has found little to be happy about in decisions supposedly reached on his behalf by those in authority at the federal level. Recent discoveries which show that protein content in grain can be successfully increased by the application of nitrogen at the proper time would indicate that farmers outside the Pal-liser triangle will be able to grow top-grade wheat under protein grading. Will these farmers be protected under the new block system? Any program, such as that under the Canada Grain Act, must be fair and equitable to all farmers, just as the initial Grain Act was. It was accepted by the producers as a boon to western agriculture when it was enacted. Let us hope now that the new act can achieve the same wide acceptance.
Has the government taken note of a resolution that was passed by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture at its annual meeting in 1969 in Quebec city which might have some bearing on the problem of income to the lower protein areas? I should like to quote as follows from one of the resolutions passed at that meeting, listed under section 8 and entitled "Grain production and grading":
(a)	Varieties
Whereas there is a potential market for nonbread wheat for human consumption as well as for livestock feeds; and
Whereas there is a need for higher yielding coarse grains;
Resolved that the Canadian plant breeding efforts be intensified toward achieving the objective of higher yielding varieties:
(a)	of grains within the present quality standards;
(b)	for higher yielding coarse grains;
(c)	for non-bread wheats for human use and livestock feed.
However that no such varieties be licensed unless such varieties are readily distinguishable from the high quality wheats presently licensed and have been adequately tested.
(b)	Grading
Whereas there seem to be far too many grades of grain in the Canadian system of grading (in the case of wheat there are over 200 grades); and
Whereas we believe that we could get along with a much smaller number of grades, thus relieving the storage problems in our elevators and terminals;

April 14. 1970
Canada Grain Act
Resolved that we request that the Board of Grain Commissioners review the present grading system with a view of reducing the number of grades.
This follows the line of some of the testimony we heard in the Standing Committee on Agriculture when we travelled across western Canada last year. At present I am in favour of a serious look being taken at our grading system, but let us not go overboard and think that it will be the complete answer.
I feel that the government has been very lax in the area of market research. This problem was emphasized a year ago last March at the conference of the Agricultural Congress when a report was tabled suggesting we were way behind some of our competitors in market research, that Canada should have a competent body which could advise farmers at least five years in advance what the consumer demand trends were likely to be for various agricultural products, and that we should govern ourselves accordingly. In other words, it is too late to close the door after the horse has been stolen. That, in effect, is what the government is now trying to do by way of a crash program.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
The Agricultural Congress suggested that we might have to cut back some wheat acreage over a ten-year period, but no suggestion was made that a program should be carried out such as the present administration is trying to force on western farmers. Like other western members, 1 have never seen our agricultural industry in the state of chaos it is in today. Farmers are faced with highest machinery costs, highest land taxes, highest interest rates, and the highest cost of living in history, not to mention the lowest returns related to input costs.
Now we find that contrary to what the minister has stated, and to add insult to injury, our neighbouring American farmers in North Dakota and Montana are stepping-up their hard wheat acreage this year by as much as 10 per cent or 15 per cent, according to some reports emanating from across the line and coming into my riding which adjoins the U.S.A. in that area. It is no wonder that our farmers are confused with a program like Operation LIFT when they see U.S.A. farmers stepping-up their production of hard wheat, laughing at Canada behind our backs while we withdraw production and fiddle around with amendments to the Grain Act instead of doing something more positive.

This bill, in the course of the next two years, may assist us in a more or less superficial way to increase wheat sales in some of the world markets, but what the government ought to be doing now is injecting at least $150 million into the western farm economy on a straight acreage payment system, with no strings attached, to tide farmers over this emergency, especially in view of the fact that grain farmers will not receive any final Wheat Board payments this spring. The government owes our farmers this, in view of its partial responsibility for the collapse of the International Wheat Agreement at the Kennedy Round talks in Geneva and for the resulting loss of wheat sales and lower prices.
My next suggestion is that another $30 million or $40 million should be immediately placed at the disposal of XCAN to set up a sales force around the world, to carry out a function similar to that undertaken by sales firms like Dreyfus, Cargills and Bungys. These sales people should be placed in about 50 countries on a salary plus commission basis, and should be supported with far more flexible trading policies, in so far as wheat is concerned, than is now the case with the Wheat Board. I want to go on record as saying that I have always supported the Wheat Board and the system of orderly marketing, but the Wheat Board can be no more effective than the government policies which back it up.
My next suggestion, which I think may be the most important, is one that I have made previously. It is that our Prime Minister, his Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp), the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister without Portfolio responsible for the Wheat Board should journey to Washington, and behind closed doors without benefit of press, radio or television discuss with President Nixon and Clifford Hardin, the U.S. Secretary of Agriculture, the very sensitive area of price-cutting under the IGA. The U.S.A. and France have been the chief offenders in this regard, and it is high time it was impressed on them that they should carry out the agreement on pricing wheat under the IGA rules. This action would not only be doing a favour to Canadian farmers but to the farmers of Australia, Argentina, France and the United States as well. The floor and ceiling prices under the original IWA worked for 18 years and can easily be made to work again if united action is taken to make them work.
April 14. 1970

I do not think for a minute that consumers expect primary producers to subsidize them by producing basic food commodities at less than cost, and I am sure that Canada cannot compete in a price war with the United States, especially when the U.S.A. consumes about 85 per cent of its wheat production whereas in Canada the figures are just the opposite.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I again emphasize that the mere changing of our grading system is no guarantee that we will automatically increase our sales of grain. I agree that we must be prepared to meet competition in highly competitive situations. If changing the act will make it easier for us to meet our customers needs, that is all to the good; but the fact still remains that the cash position of the western farmer will not improve appreciably until he can move his grain into commercial positions. Until then the farmer is going to find it increasingly difficult to finance his operations, or indeed to stay solvent under present conditions.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMISSION, PROVISIONS RESPECTING GRADING, LICENCES, ELEVATORS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am hesitant to impose on the time of the House at this stage of the bill, but I believe that on occasion more time should be taken in an effort to attract the minister's attention to the problems faced by the western grain industry, because the government does not seem to be taking any effective steps to meet the problems that exist in western Canada, problems which have resulted in a real crisis in western agriculture.
The big problem is that grain is just not selling, and nobody on the government side seems to want to talk about sales. They want to talk about inventories; they want to talk about grading; they want to talk about several other really minor items, but they refuse to get down to the basic problem which is the selling of wheat. As long as that problem is ignored, none of these other government measures will be of any use. To a large extent the low sales have been caused by the total failure of the government to handle our grain properly, and in some instances to move grain that has already been sold. We have had examples of ships coming to Canada to load grain that had been sold, but they had to leave empty because they were unable to receive their cargoes, either through sloppy labour-management relations at the terminal elevators or because the government could not properly organize the box car situation and have the grain on hand when it was
Canada Grain Act
needed. As I said at the outset, Mr. Speaker, this has resulted in a severe crisis in western Canada.
As has already been pointed out by other speakers, farmers are now getting the lowest income from grain that they have experienced in a good many years. At the same time, as is evident from the DBS figures released today, their costs have certainly not declined in proportion to their income. We now find that the government, with all its great brain power, has been successful in coming up with only two rather piddling projects to solve this major problem. The first is Operation LIFT, which I believe has been correctly lettered. I believe the National Farmers Union, instead of calling this program "Low Inventories for Tomorow" is calling it "Lower Income for Tomorrow." I think that is the proper appellation to give it because it will certainly not result in any increase in the farmers' prosperity.
In my view we are experiencing today a completely medieval approach to agricultural problems. That is what they used to do back in the Middle Ages in an effort to control the prosperity of people in Europe: they used to withhold production in order to keep prices up. Surely that is no way to approach agricultural problems today, or any of the other problems of the country. Canada needs production; it does not need restraint on production-but this is what the government has been doing with Operation LIFT. This program will not result in any injection of cash into the western farmers' pocket. In order to obtain money under it he has to do some summerfallowing; he has to pay the labour and other expenses involved in that and he also has to pay his land taxes. How will this program put extra purchasing power into his pocket?
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
I suggest that if the government was sincere about assisting the western farm economy- and I suggest they have not been sincere- they would have used the $140 million which they said they were going to inject into it, to subsidize the export of our grain. In this way we might have recovered some of the markets lost through their gross inefficiency in the handling of the agricultural affairs of this country. At one time we had 40 per cent of the world export market of grain, but it has now shrunk to 17 per cent or 18 per cent through the carelessness of this administration. One of the most effective ways to recoup our loss would be to use this money to subsidize exports.

April 14, 1970
Canada Grain Act
The government could also have made some useful changes in the quota system of grain had they been really interested in lowering the production of wheat. As the quota arrangement now exists there is a positive incentive for farmers to grow wheat. At its initial price, a bushel of wheat is worth between $1.20 and $1.25, whereas a bushel of barley for example is worth only 60 cents, yet a bushel of barley uses up the one-bushel an acre quota of the quota book the same as a bushel of wheat. The government could demonstrate its interest in wheat reduction by rewriting the quota regulations to allow farmers to grow whatever is most efficient. Certain areas of the country can grow barley much more efficiently than wheat, but the farmers are forced by government regulation to grow wheat in order to maximize the income from their land. Therefore, to a large extent we have the government artificially stimulating the production of wheat whilst at the same time trying to reduce it through the ridiculously stupid operation called LIFT. The government could do this without legislation such as Bill C-196. This is but another arm of their weapon against the farm program and against farmers in general.
Mr. Speaker, this bill will not achieve much in solving the problems of the farmer. It was heralded as a means of obtaining protein grading, but I suggest we do not need a bill the size of this one to achieve that, and I question whether it is a significant step forward in the marketing of our grain. The same result could surely be obtained by an amendment to the present legislation, the excellence of which is proven by the fact that it has remained virtually unchanged since 1930. However, it appears that the government is taking advantage of the problems created in large part by itself in order to justify the introduction of legislation such as Bill C-196.
To my mind, Mr. Speaker, this bill will go a long way toward regimenting the western farm economy. Apart from removing the control for grading of grain from this chamber to the cabinet, the bill will give the government power to licence all forms of grain handlers including truckers, railroad companies, grain elevators and feed mills. I suggest that this type of legislation is totally unnecessary and is laying the groundwork for another incursion by the government into the day-to-day affairs of its citizens. This. Mr. Speaker, is what this government seems to do at every opportunity.
I do not see any reason why the regulatory body to be established by this legislation

should be required to issue a licence to a farmer who wants to transport his grain from one province to another for the purpose of processing, when he intends to haul it back for use on his farm. As I read the bill, that power will be given to this regulatory agency.
I think that all we are doing here is expanding a bureaucracy which has already grown beyond acceptable limits. Surely the Canadian Wheat Board as presently constituted is greatly overstaffed, and savings and efficiencies could be effected there. It should look after the marketing of wheat and not be concerned with the other grains such as barley, oats, flax, rapeseed and others.
In my view, Mr. Speaker, this bill reveals the government's lack of faith in the market economy. The government does not believe that people are capable of looking after their own affairs and can plan and conduct their activities for their own advantage. The bill lays the groundwork for another large, government bureaucracy and I think this House and Canadians at large will regret the day it delegates more authority to the executive in this regard. When considering this measure the committee should be very careful not to allow these tendencies to go any further.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the last 12 years, any time the subject of agriculture has come before the House I have argued in favour of protecting the small family farm. With the large international grain market in the past I have felt, perhaps with some justification, that the large farm was in quite a good position. However, with the collapse of the world wheat agreement the whole agricultural structure of western Canada has come down in ruins. I can no longer attack this problem, therefore, from the narrow concept of giving a guaranteed income to the family farm.
I do not think this bill will get to the root of our problem though, in fairness, perhaps it is not so designed. The problem in western Canada is the collapse of international markets. The attempt to produce high quality grains may be a partial answer, and I compliment the government in this regard, but the problem is much bigger than that. I do not apologize for enlarging the thought, because this is our only opportunity to give the government the benefit of the experience of most of us from western Canada. Most of us have been raised on the farm. We have been at one time or another actively engaged in agriculture and we have had to think about it a
April 14, 1970

great deal. We have spent lots of time riding the plough or working on the farm.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
Agriculture is a way of life farming people do not want to give up. They are willing to co-operate and accept leadership of the proper kind. They are willing to take risks along with any other industry of the world, and they have done so. They have become efficient. They were told they had only to become bigger and everything would go well. These are not partisan remarks at all, because all governments so far have gone along with this policy. Farmers over the years have been encouraged to take out large loans and become bigger and more efficient. We have become efficient and now we have a large production; I will not say overproduction because I think people farming the grain fields of western Canada have a duty to perform, that of feeding a hungry world.
The problem is not just one of satisfying grain farmers and their concern for their farms. The question is, are we as a nation and is the government as a government doing everything possible to eliminate not only the grain farmer's problem but a very serious world food problem by encouraging the production of the very best, hard, red spring wheat with which this bill is intimately tied up and which can be used in eliminating hunger?
I think we have to look a little beyond this bill. We have to look at an idea which is not new; it was trotted out ten years ago and has to do with a world food bank. If we are to have a world food bank we must have storage facilities. I cannot think of a better place than Canada to store grain that is to be distributed on a worldwide basis. Mr. Speaker-I say this knowing the minister is listening-I think we should improve our grain storage facilities far beyond what they are today, especially if we look ten years ahead and pay attention to stories of the horrors of the growth in world population.
Ten years from now, instead of telling farmers to curb production we may be looking desperately for open fields and sunny places on the surface of the earth where we can grow good, hard, red spring wheat in order to feed the hungry peoples of the world who will have increased by 1.5 billion or 2 billion. They will need more food. So any long-term policy we have should look not only at immediate profits for western farmers but should examine this whole problem from
Canada Grain Act
the point of view of a world citizen. I do not think it would be idle dreaming to say that perhaps defence money could be spent, and sensibly spent, in developing a world food bank. Incidentally, a world food bank should not be concerned only with wheat; it should be concerned with pork products, fish and all other foods. Anything connected with food for humans should be integrated into a world food policy. Because this concept is relatively new and has never been tried on a global scale is no reason why Canadians should not be foremost in its development.
We cannot afford the moon race, we may not be able to afford an armaments race any more, but we can certainly make a great effort to fill the empty pantries of the world. This might be, as the world population explodes, the greatest contribution we can make and will be far better than any pious talk at the United Nations. Speaking under the shelter of the eagle's wing, we mumble about place in the world. We cannot do anything about it anyway, but we can do something about feeding people. So I think we should take a very serious view of establishing a world food bank.
This is not to say we should do less with regard to the project now being considered. I think it does not go far enough. 1 think a great deal more research must be done to determine exactly what kind of grain we should produce in future. But I am entirely opposed to the idea that we should put land back to fallow as long as there are so many hungry people in the world. I do not think it is beyond the imagination or organizing ability of the Canadian people to find a solution to both these problems at the same time. I do not think enough research has gone into our export needs.
Let us not consider our wheat only from the point of view of its high protein content or milling quality. Let us take an imaginative view of it in relation to the control of pollution. I understand, and I stand to be corrected, that if we produced a fuel for automobiles which contained 50 per cent grain alcohol, we could reduce air pollution in our cities by 75 per cent. There is an answer to the wheat surplus. No commodity is more efficiently utilized in the production of grain alcohol than wheat. It does not necessarily have to be high protein wheat. We have experience in western Canada in the production of this commodity. We might produce it on a commercial scale and surprise people. To add a little levity to my speech, in case people think

April 14. 1970
Canada Grain Act
I am being too serious, let me say that we have in Canadian industries some experience in using alcohol in this regard.
I am quite sure that grain alcohol can be produced as cheaply, if not more cheaply than gasoline. If the gasoline we are using, which is polluting our atmosphere, could be diluted with good grain alcohol, if in North America the fuel for internal combustion engines were to consist of 50 per cent grain alcohol, North America would be able to utilize the total wheat production of Canada. That is why I say this bill does not go far enough and is not as imaginative as it might be.
I mentioned storage facilities. They are important because, provided we can recover the markets we have lost and enlarge present markets along the lines I have suggested, these facilities are necessary in order to move our grain efficiently to the markets of the world. Another thing which leaps to my mind is this: we should develop more efficiency in transporting grain from the farm to storage facilities and from storage facilities, wherever they may be, to tidewater.
With unemployment rising rapidly-in this regard I disagree within the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), because I do not think unemployment in itself has any virtue-I think we would do well if we put thousands of people to work building up-to-date, modern and ultramodern facilities in transportation and in storage. In this way we would be able to compete with sellers of grain whether or not it was high protein. Of course, in most cases the storage facilities would be the same whether the grain was high or low in protein.
There is a crisis in agriculture, Mr. Speaker. I am not speaking so much about the crisis in other branches of agriculture; I am speaking primarily of the grain industry. I do not do this with any shame because that industry, so far as western Canada is concerned, is the key to the whole agricultural economy. Our farmers cannot stay in business if inflation continues to rise at the rate of 5 per cent per year. At present there is no solution for this. This is what I heard today over the radio, and I see no reason to doubt it. The farmer is not receiving, nor is he hoping for a 5 per cent increase in his selling price. There is only one way he can hope to remain in business, and that is by cutting down his overhead.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
During the past week I received several long-distance telephone calls from irate and desperate farmers concerning the loans which

we thrust upon them a few years ago. From time to time the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) and I have had verbal exchanges in the House. The minister was very keen to boast about the hundreds of millions of dollars loaned at very reasonable rates of interest in order to assist our farmers. These farmers begged me to do what I could-and goodness knows how little that is-to at least maintain the rate of interest at which they borrowed this money. In a great many cases they have no income whatsoever, yet the interest rate on government guaranteed loans is being increased by the banks from 3J per cent to 7 per cent more than the original rate. No such boasts were made in this House, on the hustings or in the Department of Agriculture generally when the farmers were encouraged to take advantage of farm loans and participate in our growing agricultural industry. These farmers now face a situation of no markets and an increasing interest rate on loans. They are desperate and have asked me to do something about it. What can I do but appeal to this House, through Your Honour, and ask that something be done? These farmers believe we can do something. They believe we have the right to set interest rates because of the change in the ceiling of interest rates a year or so ago.
At that time the public was informed that if we removed the ceiling on interest rates, money would flow freely into the proper channels and people who needed loans would be able to borrow at a reasonable interest rate. Money was being loaned at exorbitant interest rates by the loan sharks. I am receiving long-distance telephone calls from farmers complaining that the government is not renewing their loans at the original 5 per cent or 6 per cent rate of interest; the banks are now demanding 8J per cent to 12 per cent interest. In some cases, because they are in financial straits, farmers must obtain permission from the minister to renew their loan so that the banks will not foreclose. Farmers who have some security in mixed farming are being forced to sell their cattle because they cannot sell their grain. This is necessary to pay off the loans which were obtained only a few months ago when the government was boasting about the hundreds of millions of dollars available to the people of Canada. The farmers were told that they never had it so good. Apart from droughts and acts of God, the farmers never had it so bad!
Farmers were encouraged to become larger in operation and more efficient. They were urged to purchase the farms of inefficient
April 14, 1970

neighbours, to plow the land more efficiently and to use fertilizers, which were bought with cash. It is not necessary to be Jeremiah to see that these people are now starving in the midst of plenty. They owe "x" number of dollars, no money is being earned and the banks are asking to be paid. These people are becoming alarmed.
Are we to assume that the financial institutions of Canada have more influence on this House than farmers who are in these terrible straits? Parliament encouraged these people to get into this unenviable position. Some of these farmers had a small quarter-section of land; the mother and the children helped with the chores. They were encouraged to become more efficient and to grow more bushels per acre of better quality grain. They were told that this benevolent government would see to it that everything would be fine.
For 12 years I have been begging the government to obtain markets. The government has become deeply embroiled in the agricultural industry and is now telling farmers how to run their business, even though they know a great deal more about it than the government. I suggest it is time for the government to pick up the tab. Anyone can make sales when you have unlimited markets. It is possible to make money selling hot-dogs to a large crowd of fairgoers on a sunny day. However, the storm clouds of competition are now upon us. World markets are no longer forced to rely upon us; they have become very competitive.
It is necessary to streamline our policies. We must do more than produce high quality grain. We must do a great deal more than simply amend the regulations which state how the grain shall qualify for market. We need salesmen. These salesmen should be in a position to sell good quality wheat at reasonable, world prices. It must be worth while for our farmers to produce grain. If the world wheat agreement has broken down, we are a free agent and can no longer rely on that agreement. We must determine whether Canada will again participate in a world wheat agreement. If the old agreement is out of date, I suggest there should be a new one along the lines I have mentioned. It should be based on the need to fill hungry stomachs. Canada can pioneer in this field. This can be compared with defence: it is better to spend a billion dollars a year to feed hungry people than manufacture useless weapons of war, nerve gases and all the other things necessary
Canada Grain Act
for the game of war. This game is tied up with the subsidizing of privately-owned factories producing weapons of war.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
Any institution that is conducive to poverty in this country is a menace. In this regard I think a great deal more homework must be done. From the short-term point of view I would suggest to the Minister of Agriculture that he convene a national conference of farmers to decide just where the farmers are going in agriculture today, what should be our long-term policy, what should be our world policy in agriculture, what our national policy is going to be, our provincial policy, and what the farmers themselves are going to do about all this. Any negative policy that asks farmers not to be farmers will not work. A policy must be devised, even at the eleventh hour, that will show the farmers how they fit into their job of producing food for people. If we are sincere, I think problems of price, storage, transportation and grading will fall into their proper place.
I firmly believe that there is and always will be a great future for agriculture. I believe that the efficient farmer is the man who loves his job and his land the farmer who is more interested in his way of life than in so-called dollar efficiency; the farmer who finds farming the most satisfying way to earn his daily bread. I suggest any government policy that tells farmers to leave their land fallow is inadequate even in the short-term, and certainly over the long-term. It is not only against humanity but against nature. When policies are inhuman and do not take into account human values, when your policies try to put dollar efficiency ahead of enriching individual human life, such policies are doomed to failure. If your policies put human values first along with quality of life, I think you will find that those little problems of financing and marketing, efficiency and distribution, storage and so on will find their rightful place.
Having observed the evolution of agricultural policies over the past 12 years, I have come to the conclusion that we have been on the wrong track. More and more we have had government interference, the taking over of land by the state and the adoption of an inhuman, unrealistic approach to farming. You cannot conduct a farming operation in any country unless you have the man on the soil. I know of no way to force a man to be a good farmer. Farming is a way of life. It is

April 14, 1970
Canada Grain Act
man's oldest profession and is one of man's noblest professions. When a heartless state takes over the responsibility of telling farmers what they will grow, how they will grow it and where they will sell what they grow, farming becomes no longer a profession but just another form of slavery. Under such circumstances farming is not worth the long hours that are required. It is not worth facing the weather and taking a gamble, pitting yourself against nature and your intelligence against the elements, endeavouring through good times and bad to produce the best and the cheapest food.
I suggest we have not given enough thought to the future of farming. We have given too much thought to making the farmers farm our way. This approach does not work. If you lend a farmer money, if you force him to borrow money, I think you have the duty to see that he is able to repay that loan. If you ask him to be efficient, do not criticize him when he becomes efficient. We have asked our farmers to expand their operations, and they have expanded. All the farmers ask now is that the government, which already has interfered too much in their way of life, present them with a reasonable program to protect the financial position in which they find themselves.
I suggest that the government should keep faith with the farmers and let them repay the money lent to them at the original interest rate of the loan. Secondly, our agricultural policy in all phases should reflect positive rather than negative thinking. We must find some way of making the land productive and able to pay its way. The suggestion of putting certain Wheatland which perhaps should never have been plowed back into grass is sound, but even this must be done carefully. The price of grass seed today on the Prairies has skyrocketed. Even if the farmer wanted to return his land to grass and take advantage of what I think was a well-meant program, this is almost beyond his financial grasp. If a farmer already owes money, by the time he has bought grass seed at exorbitant prices he will owe a lot more. In most cases it just cannot be done.
The government is making an effort to pump money back into the Prairies. This is the reason no member from the Prairies has stood up and said that he wants nothing to do with this program. I think all western members are hopeful that there will be some positive help given by the passage of this bill. Certainly I think improvement in grading of

grain will assist. I also think we should give the farmers an incentive of some kind to produce the high quality grain that will sell on the limited market that we have. In addition to this I beg the minister to take a much broader and imaginative look, I might even say a daring look, at our agricultural policies, and to turn back the pages of time and adopt a natural attitude to farming, a natural trust of individual farmers, their old-fashioned thrift and their self-sufficiency.
When offering the farmers a loan, I would say that the best advice of all is to tell them not to take it unless they need it very badly. But if in its kindness the government does make a loan available to the farmers, I hope they will keep their good faith and allow the farmers to repay it at the same interest rate as the original loan, particularly in times like these when they find it very hard to exist and to keep their families on the land they love.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-196 is another move by the government to try to do something about a problem which is becoming difficult. As I see it, this is an attempt to regulate the handling of grain, the movement of grain and the juggling around and trying to regulate in some way the grading of grain. Having looked at this bill, I think it would be very fair to say that it really is not aimed in the direction in which our agricultural problems lie. This bill misses the boat. The real problem relates to the loss of our markets in the world. Markets for wheat have been dropping continuously ever since the Liberals took power, not too long ago. A few years ago Canada possessed about 33 per cent of the world wheat market. That position has now slipped to approximately 17 per cent.
At the present time there is a surplus of wheat in the world of 2 billion bushels or a little more. We also know that half or more of this surplus exists in our own country; half of that world surplus is in Canada. If we look a little further into the problem to determine who are the wheat producers of the world, we find that Canada produces only about 5 per cent of the world's wheat. What does this reflect-this loss of sales from 33 per cent to 17 per cent, with half the world's wheat surplus in a country that produces only 5 per cent of the world's wheat? The situation is getting progressively worse day by day, yet the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) sits back reading a newspaper while a speech on this very important topic is being made.

This indicates that the minister may not think the problem is as serious as it really is. Part of his suggestion is to change the grading of wheat from the old system to a protein grading system. Nowhere in the bill does it say how he is going to do this, who is going to do it or where the physical facilities needed for this type of grading are located. What is the use of passing a bill that cannot be implemented? What is the use of introducing a grading system for which no physical facilities exist at the present time? I see this as just another snow job or smokescreen to cover inactivity. It gives people something to talk about but does not offer any real, concrete solution to the problem we face.
In the past five or six years in my own area half of the farmers have quit farming. They have quit because the economy of the farm has become more and more difficult. The farmers' income has been dropping continuously at an accelerated rate, particularly since 1962. Farmers are leaving the farms at the rate of about 10 per cent a year. If we carry this to its logical conclusion, how many farmers will we have five or six years from now? We must remember that we are losing 10 per cent per year and we have lost 5 per cent to 10 per cent per year in the last five years. Even more farmers are being uprooted from their homes. They are leaving the farms to go to the cities, or moving to towns.
These people have spent years working the soil and trying to eke out an honest living. Their reward in this country is a move to town at age 55 to try to get a job as a janitor sweeping somebody's floors, so they can make a living until they reach the age at which they can draw the old age pension. That is not a very colourful picture, but it is what we have in this country today. I hope the Minister of Agriculture, who is a farmer, does no face that prospect when he reaches age 55, assuming he is not 55 now.
What are the reasons for this difficult situation? I think they are very obvious. In the past 20 years the price of farm produce has remained the same or has dropped. The price of wheat, for example, is lower now than it was in 1950. The price of beef and hogs is about the same, or maybe a little less at times: it does fluctuate, but for all intents and purposes we can say it is about the same. Let us compare the price of farm machinery in the same period. What is the price of a trac-22218-25

We have a situation in which gross income has stayed about the same. The price of produce has not increased; it has remained roughly the same or has decreased a little. These matters are extremely important and they are very closely related to the bill we are discussing. I want to make a few comments about the LIFT program, which stands for "Lower Income For Tomorrow" for farmers. What the minister and his colleague from Saskatoon are doing is asking the farmer to give up one year of his income. I wonder what other group in this country

April 14, 1970
Canada Grain Act
would tolerate that. What other group of people would sit back and accept the government's suggestion that they quit work this year and take a holiday without pay. This business about $6 per acre for working the land is a big hoax: in most cases it will not cover the cost involved in summerfallow.
The publicity given to the LIFT program and giving the farmer a holiday with pay is a big laugh. The government, is just asking the farmer to give up a year's salary. They disregard the fact that almost every farmer has tremendous debts and that they have been getting progressively deeper and deeper into debt during the past several years. Their income has progressively decreased. We are now asking them to completely give up their income for a year. The government is not making any suggestion as to how farmers will meet their payments to the banks and the farm machinery companies, or in respect of farm improvement loans or, for that matter, to the grocer. I know of some farmers in Alberta who do not even have access to credit at the grocery store any longer because they are so deeply in debt. Their prospects are extremely grim.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
If the government is truly concerned about trying to do something in respect of the agricultural problem, from the point of view of solving the wheat surplus and at the same time assisting all the farmers, I think it could come up with something a lot more original than simply asking the farmers to stop growing wheat. If it cannot come up with something original, it could look back at the situation in the years when the Conservatives were in power. It could learn something from that. When agricultural conditions were difficult at that time, they gave the farmers an acreage payment. When the crops were snowed under, they gave them a snowed under bonus. Every farmer who has been in the west for some time would say that the Conservative years were good years for them. It is a well-known fact that Liberal years have not been good years.

speechtext:
Yes, Liberal years are lean years; that is a good slogan. If the government truly wants to spend the $140 million it indicates it has available, I think it should try to help the farmer in a better way. One way would be to provide an acreage payment. They could use a few dollars as an acreage payment, but I think more importantly the

government should re-establish Canada's position on the world market. We should increase our sales rather than stop producing. This is a simple solution. It just requires a little action. But for some reason the government seems to ignore this very simple suggestion.
There are several ways in which new markets could be gained. One would be to subsidize the price of wheat. This would allow us to recapture a good deal of the world market in which Canada has been undersold by other countries. We could use some of the LIFT money to do this. We could try to get back the 33 per cent of the wheat market we had during the Conservative years. We might also try to advertise a little. We should set up a marketing agency concerned solely with the marketing of Canadian wheat.
I think these suggestions would prove to be very useful if the government attempted to implement them. I have been a member of the House for only two years, but that short period of time is long enough for me to notice that the Liberal government bounces from crisis to crisis. It does not seem to be able to look at a problem and predict that it may become worse. The government does not seem to recognize the seriousness of a problem in time to bring in a policy to prevent a crisis occurring. The Minister of Agriculture and the government just will not do that.
I think the Minister of Agriculture knows the problem pertaining to farming. Being a farmer himself, he should know the problem. But I wonder why he does not do something useful in an attempt to solve it. When he was appointed Minister of Agriculture as his just reward for joining the party in power, we thought maybe this would be pretty good. We thought here is a man, a farmer himself and an Albertan, who is very familiar with the western agricultural problem and we were looking forward to a good deal of relief for western farmers.
I am sorry to say that not only I but all the farmers I know, and many whom I do not know, have been extremely disappointed because in spite of the fact that the agricultural minister is familiar with the farming problem, he repeatedly refuses to develop long-term and intermediate policies which would pull the farmer out of the terrible mire in which he now wades. Let us, for example, briefly summarize what the minister has done in the past few years to help the farmer improve his income situation and his standard of living. The first thing was to increase the
April 14, 1970

interest rate on farm credit loans. I think the Minister of Agriculture thought this was a good thing for the farmers, but I am not sure it was. Another thing he did was increase the amount a farmer could borrow. Perhaps that is all right in some respects, but all it really did was get the farmer deeper in debt. The ability to borrow more money by itself is of no value unless the ability to repay the debt is also developed. This is the most important thing.
To date the Minister of Agriculture has done absolutely nothing to increase the ability of the farmer to repay his loan. That is why I repeat the old slogan that the Liberal years are bad years. What we need in this country is a return to a Conservative government. I do not say that with partisan feeling, but because I feel it would be good for agriculture in the west and in the east.
If I might return for a moment to the LIFT program, recently I conducted a survey among farmers who are friends of mine, in a fairly large area of northern Alberta. It is very obvious that the LIFT program is a sham. It will not help many farmers in the area I surveyed. As a matter of fact, in a radius of 50 miles not one farmer said that he would benefit from this program. So it is just another snow job on the public. It is another cover up for the inactivity of the government and its inability to sell wheat, as well as its general inability to cope with an agricultural problem which progressively has become worse over the past few years.
I think the Minister of Agriculture should be able to do a little better than he has. I know he is intelligent. As I said, he is a farmer himself and I think he knows the problem. He is the minister responsible, and therefore I ask why he repeatedly lets us down and sits idly by as the agricultural industry day by day slips slowly down the drain.

speakeroldname: Hon. H. A. Olson (Minister of Agriculture) moved
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL MARKETING COUNCIL AND AGENCIES
speechtext:
that Bill C-197, to establish the National Farm Products Marketing Council and to authorize the establishment of national marketing agencies for farm products, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Agriculture.
He said: Mr. Speaker, Bill C-197 is a very important and new departure in federal legislation. I intend to deal more specifically with the objectives of this act and indeed some of the specific provisions in the act within the next few minutes. However, I would like to set the preamble to that discussion by making the comment that the situation we have respecting the marketing of foreign products in Canada, in my view at least, makes it at least desirable if not essential that we have enabling legislation on the statute books, that is, authority from Parliament for the government to respond from time to time to the requests of a substantial majority of producers in this field.
The farming industry of Canada is made up of over 400,000 individual farmers all of whom are making decisions, in many cases independently of one another. Over the years governments have considered it essential to provide the legislative framework which would make it possible for farmers to work
IMr. Olson.]

together in solving some of their problems. This is particularly important with respect to farmers' efforts in marketing the products of the farm in today's highly organized economy.
I think it is important that we place our agricultural industry in a position to improve our marketing systems. Rapid improvements in production methods and capability, combined with increasing complexity and diversity of the markets for farm products, underline the importance of expanding and improving our efforts in the field of marketing.
There are serious problems in the agricultural industry associated with fluctuations in farm income mainly due to instability of product prices. There are undoubtedly opportunities to expand markets. Hon. members referred to this from time to time in the course of the debate just ended. There are opportunities, I suggest, to improve the efficiency of our marketing systems. There are wide fluctuations in the supply of products which are available for marketing. Producers are investing more and more money and know-how in production facilities and production programs. Therefore I think it is important that we provide for some form of national co-ordination of these marketing programs.
I think it would be appropriate for me to give some historical background. For example, the federal government introduced fairly broad marketing legislation in the early 1930s. This legislation was later ruled by the courts to be ultra vires or outside federal jurisdiction. Since then provincial governments have implemented marketing legislation which has enabled producers to organize a number of provincial marketing boards, agencies and commissions-several other names have been attached to these-under the authority of the provincial marketing legislation.
About half of Canada's farm products today are marketed under the aegis of some type of provincial or federal marketing agency. But the provinces and the producers generally have been frustrated in their attempts to do an effective job of the orderly marketing of farm products, that is, working through individual, provincially organized marketing bodies, and the need for national legislation of the type which we have set before you has become evident.
April 14, 1970

[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
I will refer to this a little later, but over the last two years there has been a series of meetings which I attended-and indeed there were meetings before that-where provincial ministers met with the federal minister and the Department of Agriculture with a view to putting some co-ordinating measure in place at the national level which would allow these provincial boards, and additional marketing structures for other commodities, to be more effective in achieving the desired result, which is a uniform price structure and stability for producers.
In the past provision was made through specific legislation for marketing agencies under the jurisdiction of the federal government. An outstanding example of this is the Canadian Wheat Board. But we have concluded that there is now need for legislative authority which places the federal government in a position to design structures and orderly marketing programs to deal with specific but greatly varying circumstances related to different farm commodities.
The constitution provides the federal government with authority for the general overseeing of the marketing of farm products in interprovincial and international trade, and the provinces with authority over marketing of farm products within a province. National structures must therefore relate closely to the provinces and to the provincial marketing boards where they exist. In a sense, therefore, Mr. Speaker, this legislation provides for a bridging of the jurisdiction in this very important area. The provinces, for example, may delegate responsibility over intraprovincial marketing to agencies established under this legislation. The complexity of this jurisdictional question, the varying circumstances associated with different products and the need for taking action promptly when it is appropriate to do so all underline the importance of the Governor in Council having authority to proceed under the mandate which this legislation will provide.
The legislation also provides for the establishment of a National Farm Products Marketing Council. This council will be a very important body. Operating under this legislation it will provide guidance and advice in the first instance as to whether or not a scheme should be considered. It will basically determine the nature of schemes which are to * be considered under this legislation and will carry the responsibility for continuing scruti-
Farm Products Marketing Agencies Bill ny and guidance of agencies which are established under the legislation.
The council will also have the responsibility of maintaining very close liaison with provincial marketing councils and with provincial governments generally. It will have among its functions the promotion of improvement of marketing of farm products in Canada. The legislation vests with the council the responsibility to assure that the policies of agencies which are carried out are such as to maintain and promote an efficient and competitive agricultural industry. It is also their responsibility to have in mind not only the interests of the producers but also of the consumers and others who are interested in the farm product which is being marketed.
The council will hold public hearings before recommending any plans. This is in order to assure that all interested parties have an opportunity to study and to consider proposed marketing plans and to make their views known with regard to them. I do not * see the formation of national marketing agencies as a panacea for all our problems but, Mr. Speaker, on the other hand this legislation does mark real progress in placing us in a position to respond to requests for specific marketing schemes that are designed to provide improvements through national agencies for specific commodities.
As said a few moments ago, the objective of this legislation is to provide for more effective marketing of farm products by placing the federal government in a position to respond to and to create national marketing agencies for specific commodities as the need arises. For example, this bill will provide for the establishment by the Governor in Council of a National Farm Products Marketing Council, which will provide advice with respect to the establishment of and supervision over the operation of specific commodity agencies established under this bill. The bill will also provide for the establishment by the Governor in Council of national marketing agencies authorized to administer an approved marketing plan related to a designated farm product or farm products.
Due to the nature of the organization of the farming industry, with a great many producers making individual decisions, it has been accepted that the producers should have the opportunity to organize for more orderly marketing of their products. To a large degree the provinces have proceeded to implement farm products marketing legislation providing for the establishment of producer
April 14, 1970
5870	COMMONS DEBATES
Farm Products Marketing Agencies Bill
marketing boards, and more recently for other types of farm product marketing agencies as well. As a matter of fact, there are now approximately 120 provincial or sub-provincial marketing agencies in operation across Canada.
It has become evident to producers that there is a further need for a national approach to such marketing schemes, at least for some of the commodities, because of the limited effectiveness of segmented and uncoordinated provincial schemes. In addition, there is good reason to provide for national leadership in this area having regard for the interests of the economy and the efficient use of resources devoted to agriculture in the various regions of Canada. Without legislation such as this, producer groups and provinces could place the onus for lack of co-ordinated action in the marketing field on the federal government, and indeed they have done so.
As I said, over the last 24 months we had a number of meetings with them dealing with this matter. As I have also said, the bill provides the Governor in Council with the authority to establish agencies which would exercise some or all of the federal powers over the marketing of a named farm commodity within a region or within all of Canada. The Governor in Council could approve a specific marketing plan and appoint an agency which would be authorized to administer the plan. The bill thus provides for the design of specific marketing schemes tailored to the requirements and the peculiarities or particular commodities, and such schemes of course could be approved individually by the Governor in Council.
On the one hand, the agencies established under this bill could be granted very limited powers as necessary to achieve a minimum co-ordination, or promotional function. On the other hand, a range of powers could be granted as appropriate to carrying out a more comprehensive marketing function, including such things as selling, pricing, assembling, packing, processing, transporting and the storing of designated products involved in interprovincial and export trade.
The marketing agencies established by the Governor in Council would be in the position, on the concurrence of the Minister of Agriculture, to receive a delegation of powers from provinces in order that the agencies would be a in position to exercise provincial as well as federal authority over the marketing of a designated farm product or products. The federal government generally has juris-
diction over the interprovincial and export movement of products, and the provinces over the marketing of products within a province.
The bill also provides for the appointment by the Governor in Council of a National Farm Products Marketing Council. This council will have considerable responsibility with respect to the design, review and the overseeing of the operation of marketing plans and of marketing agencies established under this legislation. Considerable emphasis is placed in the bill on the maintenance and expansion of an economic and competitive farming industry, and on a dependable supply of high quality products to the consumer. The council is vested with the prime responsibility for determining that such plans are in the interests of the agricultural industry and have regard for other sectors of the economy, including the consumer.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
Mr. Speaker, in conclusion I should like to advise hon. members that there have been extensive discussions with a member of producer organizations, particularly the poultry producers, who are most anxious that the government establish a structure that will enable them to set up a national marketing agency. It has been decided to proceed with general legislation rather than with specific commodity legislation, and the nature of this bill and the support for it has been indicated by producers during these meetings.
In addition, the matter has been discussed with other more general farm organizations and groups of farmers and other interested persons. The indication is that there is a general support, and in some cases very strong support for this type of legislation rather than some of the other objectives that would be open to us. I want to repeat that the matter has been discussed in detail with the provinces at both the ministerial and official level, first in the context of the specific request that came forward, for example, from the poultry industry and more recently in the context of the proposal to provide this enabling legislation. I should say that the provinces generally support this type of legislation. Indeed, much of it was designed because of the essential nature of their participation, in line with some of the suggestions they made to us.
Mr. Speaker, this legislation does not directly affect any other bill or policy that I am aware of. It is, however, closely related to the Agricultural Products Marketing Act which provides for delegation of federal
April 14. 1970
COMMONS DEBATES	5871
Farm. Products Marketing Agencies Bill
powers to similar provincial boards, a practice which has been used many times in the past.
With respect to international ramifications, the bill does not provide the opportunity to give marketing agencies established under it direct or, indeed, automatic control over the importation of agricultural products. In certain circumstances authority could be delegated to these agencies, but I should like to make it clear that Bill C-197 does not automatically provide the exercise of control in international trade.
The bill has very important federal-provincial ramifications, as marketing of farm products is an area that is under both federal and provincial jurisdiction. I have said that we see no serious problems in that regard due to the extensive consultations with the provincial authorities and to the provisions in the act for agencies established thereunder to receive delegation of provincial powers and to name bodies established under provincial legislation as agents, within a province, of the national marketing agency.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that many farm organizations in Canada have waited a long time for this kind of legislation. I should like to conclude by suggesting to hon. members, and indeed to Canadian farmers generally who think that national marketing legislation is as simple as providing the authority for somebody to set production quotas and prices, that in my view this will not solve the problem of the marketplace. That has been tried without success and is one extreme in the attitude toward national marketing agencies. The other extreme is to shy away from any suggestion of marketing boards, commissions or agencies and have nothing to do with any kind of structure that would give the producers greater influence in the marketplace.
In my view, Mr. Speaker, the adamant refusal to recognize that producers, and particularly farmers, ought to have a greater influence in the marketplace through their own efforts is also wrong. Had I time I could name specific commodities which experienced difficulty because of lack of co-ordinated effort between producers and where in retrospect it would have been possible to have had a more uniform price structure had there been some co-ordination of effort under the aegis of this kind of legislation. In its absence there were, instead, very depressed prices throughout the whole marketing season notwithstanding an excess of supply and market demand. Either extreme position is wrong, in
my view. We have to find some area in
between where national marketing agencies are not so compulsory, where they have not only one thing on their minds and that is to set production quotas and prices. There must be an area in between for co-ordination amongst producers.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that in this area of supply management-a term which is being overused these days and which does not relate only to production-a great deal of benefit could flow to farmers if there was a co-ordinated agency which could manage the flow of production into the marketplace in relation to what the market could absorb on a daily, weekly or even on a monthly basis.
I hope hon. members of this House will give this legislation careful consideration with these concepts in mind. It could become a useful instrument in assisting agricultural producers in Canada to have a greater influence in the marketplace for their own benefit and indeed for the stability of the industry all across Canada.

I do not think the minister ought to expect this type of legislation to go through without someone in this country being aroused, because I certainly read it differently from the way the minister reads it. I wish I could say to our people, "Mr. Farmer, Mr. Businessman, Mr. whoever you may be, Mr. Canadian, look at Bill C-197, because that is a good indication of where this government is going." I have never been licensed to produce anything, but this bill does that. It says if you [Mr. Korchinski.)
have no licence to produce certain things, you can be put in jail for two years. That is what the bill provides. My God! Where art thou, my God? Surely you will have compassion on us, because this government certainly has none.

An inspector may at any reasonable time enter any place, other than a private dwelling place or any part of a place that is designed to be used and is being used as a permanent or temporary private dwelling place, in which he reasonably believes there is any regulated product produced for, or intended to be marketed in, interprovincial or export trade and may examine any books, records or other documents in such place that on reasonable grounds he believes contain any information relating to the regulated product and make copies thereof of extracts therefrom.

AGRICULTURE-FEED GRAIN-REQUESTED INCREASE IN FREIGHT RATE ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope the House will not be unnerved by my standing up to take part in a debate on agriculture. Having managed to survive Hon. Paul Martin's discovery of the soybean, the House can probably survive my remarks as well. I speak on behalf of 9,500 farms in Nova Scotia. I speak of a problem, however, which affects not only my own provinces but all other provinces. It has to do with feed freight assistance. I have no quarrel, really, with the answer that brought us here. The minister gave as full an answer as could be given on the Orders of the Day, but I think it would be very helpful if he would elaborate on this question when he replies to me in a few minutes' time.
Let me relate the dimensions of the problem. Nova Scotia in 1965 grew 17 per cent of the grain for its own consumption, and in 1950 it grew 32 per cent of what it consumed in total. So that looking over the figures which are supplied to me by the Nova Scotia Federation of Agriculture, it is clear that for the last 20 or 25 years roughly 80 per cent of the grain needed for Nova Scotia farmers has had to be imported.
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
On Saturday night I spoke to a group of people in the farming industry. They asked that this matter be raised in Parliament. I understand that the farming industry is affected in this order. About 80 per cent of the expense in the pork industry is for grain, and about 70 per cent of the expense in the chicken industry is for grain. I pause to point out that both these farming endeavours can be carried out on non-productive land; that is, hogs and chickens are penned and fed. The 22218-26

In other words, the dairy farmer would have an opportunity if some other program were substituted which would help him to clear land thereby enabling him to grow grain to feed the livestock. However, the farmer who produces swine or raises chickens would not be in the same position. The Maritime Federation of Agriculture has pinpointed the problem in this way:
Whereas Maritime farmers import in excess of 50 per cent of the feed grains, used in these provinces and, whereas the poultry and broiler industry rely almost entirely on imported feed grains, and
whereas the dairy, beef and hog phases of agriculture in the Maritimes are in an expansion program based to a large degree on imported feed grains, and

whereas the government of Canada is seeking to eradicate the regional disparities in Canada, and more especially, to eradicate the regional disparity between the Atlantic region of Canada and the Ontario-Quebec region of Canada.

Therefore be it resolved that the government of Canada be requested to provide adequate funds to the Canadian Livestock Feed Board so that the rates of feed freight equalization can be restored and maintained at the 1962 levels and that vegetable proteins be included in the program.

speakeroldname: Hon. H. A. Olson (Minister of Agriculture):
maintopic: AGRICULTURE-FEED GRAIN-REQUESTED INCREASE IN FREIGHT RATE ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to cover as much ground as I can during the three minutes at my disposal, but to give a detailed explanation in reply to the number of comments and questions raised by the hon. member would be impossible in that length of time. I should advise the hon. member that making estimates with respect to a program such as feed freight assistance is very difficult. This is an open-ended program under which we offer to pay a certain number of dollars per ton of total volume offered for movement, for example from Thunder Bay and other places in Ontario farther east, in any year.
Last year we had a situation where there was a significant upswing in the total volume of feed grain coming into certain parts of Ontario, and indeed into the Maritime provinces, in substitution for what had been supplied through production of Ontario grain in the past. As a result, the government ran into additional expense. When we realized this was happening to a very large degree in September, 1969, we made some adjustments. We adjusted the rates into many areas, but primarily we wanted to equalize the disparities that had shown up between various zones as a result of changes in transportation costs.
What we want is a form of equalized payment so that the balance of the payments that a livestock feeder has to pay, whether $2 a ton or $3 a ton out of the ten, is reasonably the same for all. However, when transportation costs change, this does become distorted. Another thing we did was to add by way of a supplementary estimate another $1 million, raising the total amount from $221.5 million to $222.5 million, to take care of the increased volume. I also realize there were reductions in the rates that had an affect in all areas from Ontario to the Maritimes.
So far as the amount for 1970-71 is concerned, it is true that this is down, from a total expenditure of $22.5 million in 1969-70 to an estimated expenditure of $17.6 million in 1970-71. We have not changed the rates. It is too early at this point in time to be able to predict with any accuracy how much will be brought forward for this feeding season. However, that is a matter we will have to look at as we see what the total supplies of locally grown grain from Ontario, Quebec or the Maritimes amount to, and this will not be known until later.
So far as the long-range plans are concerned, I am aware that ministers ought not to give commitments extending far into the future committing future ministers as well, indeed, as future Parliaments and governments. However, as far as I am concerned- and I have said this many times across the country-I think feed freight assistance is a good, sound, economic program for Canadians both in the grain producing area and in the livestock feeding area; in other words, at both ends.
